articles.summary: US and Israel are warned against launching fresh strikes on Iran  The GuardianIstanbul meeting: A new division of labor in the Iran war?  Iran InternationalEuropean, Middle East ministers urge US-Iran diplomacy, not new attacks  Al JazeeraTurkey says renewed attack on Iran would expand conflict, diplomacy only way  ReutersEgypt, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Pakistan say 'Israeli occupation main source of regional instability'  The Times of Israel
articles.full_text:
Foreign ministers at a summit of eight European and Middle Eastern countries have urged the US and Israel not to renews their attacks on Iran, warning a fresh outbreak of fighting would spread conflict and push oil prices even higher.
The development of a new multinational “anti-war bloc” represents a challenge to the increasingly open plans by the US and Israel to relaunch strikes on Iran while talks on Tehran’s nuclear programme remain deadlocked.
The Turkish foreign minister, Hakan Fidan, joint convener of the summit in Istanbul, said: “Military intervention in Iran is not any kind of solution. We agreed that a new military attack would spread the war and the conflict in the region. All the countries around the table do not want the war to spread even more, once again.”
Ministers also demanded an end to the Houthi assaults on Saudi Arabia, and an immediate opening of the strait of Hormuz currently blockaded by Iranian ships and drones.
Jean-Noël Barrot, the French foreign minister, said another war between Iran and the US would be bad for both sides, and only worsen rising oil prices, which have hit their highest level since May. Ed Miliband, the UK foreign secretary, also urged both sides to embrace diplomacy.
The Istanbul meeting, an unprecedented gathering of regional and European leaders initiated by Turkey and Germany, represented a rare chance for European ministers to have any input into the crises afflicting the Middle East, including in Yemen, Palestine and Iran. They have largely been left as bystanders, apart from sending air force protection to Saudi Arabia as it tries to fend off Houthi drone and missile assaults on its airports and energy installations.
The Middle Eastern states were represented by Fidan, Egypt’s Badr Abdelatty, Pakistan’s Ishaq Dar and Saudi Arabia’s Faisal bin Farhan. Pakistan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia formed the Mecca defensive security pact in August, a grouping Egypt may join.
The European side was represented by Barrot, Miliband, Germany’s Johann Wadephul and Italy’s Antonio Tajani. The agenda covered the Palestinian issue, including settlement expansion, settler violence and the two-state solution, as well as security in the strait of Hormuz, Yemen and efforts to end the Russia-Ukraine war and prevent spillover into the Black Sea.
Wadephul said: “We are united by the impact these deadlocked conflicts are having on the economy and security of our countries and by the will to seek new ways to bring about solutions.”
He made no criticism of the US but accused “the Houthis and Iran of blackmailing world trade and continuing to stranglehold global supplies of energy and fertiliser”.
“We are feeling the effects of the attacks on shipping routes and whether at the petrol pump or the supermarket,” he said. “Elsewhere there is threat of famine.”
Tajani said the aim of the meeting was to work for “de-escalation to guarantee freedom of navigation”.
“I do not believe the problem can be solved from a purely military standpoint,” he added. “If we want to reopen Hormuz, which is vital for our economies, we must promote dialogue and make Iran understand that this attitude cannot continue.”

articles.title: QatarEnergy Signs Long-Term Deal to Buy U.S. LNG as Iran War Disrupts Exports - gCaptain
articles.summary: QatarEnergy Signs Long-Term Deal to Buy U.S. LNG as Iran War Disrupts Exports  gCaptain
articles.full_text:
QatarEnergy has signed two long-term agreements to purchase up to 4 million tonnes of U.S. liquefied natural gas annually from Cheniere Energy through 2054, as the Gulf producer continues to grapple with damage to its own export facilities from the war with Iran.
The agreements, announced Thursday, cover 2 million tonnes per annum (MTPA) each from Cheniere’s Sabine Pass facility in Louisiana and Corpus Christi facility in Texas. Deliveries are expected to begin in 2031 and continue through 2054.
Under the contracts, QatarEnergy will purchase the LNG on a free-on-board (FOB) basis, taking responsibility for transporting cargoes from the U.S. terminals. Pricing will be linked to the Henry Hub natural gas benchmark plus a fixed fee.
The deal comes as QatarEnergy faces significant disruptions to its own LNG production following Iranian missile strikes on its Ras Laffan Industrial City in March.
The attacks damaged two LNG production trains with a combined capacity of 12.8 MTPA, knocking out approximately 17% of Qatar’s export capacity. QatarEnergy has warned that repairs could take three to five years, potentially costing $20 billion annually in lost revenue and disrupting long-term supply commitments to customers in Europe and Asia.
While the U.S. contracts will not begin delivering cargoes until the early 2030s, they will give QatarEnergy an additional source of supply outside the Persian Gulf, where energy infrastructure and shipping have faced mounting threats during the conflict.
QatarEnergy described the agreements as part of its broader strategy to diversify its global LNG portfolio.
“This major long-term purchase will expand and diversify our global LNG portfolio and advance our ability to meet the evolving requirements of the market,” said Saad Sherida Al-Kaabi, Qatar’s minister of state for energy affairs and CEO of QatarEnergy.
For Cheniere, the agreements secure another major long-term customer for its U.S. Gulf Coast operations.
The company currently operates approximately 56 MTPA of LNG production capacity across Sabine Pass and Corpus Christi, with another 5 MTPA under construction. One million tonnes annually under the new Sabine Pass agreement remains contingent on a final investment decision for the first phase of the terminal’s planned expansion.
The deal highlights QatarEnergy’s growing role not only as a major LNG producer but also as an international LNG trader, while adding another long-term source of U.S. Gulf Coast cargoes that can reach global markets without passing through the Strait of Hormuz.

articles.title: From the mountains of Yemen to the regional stage: the rise of the Houthis with the support of Iran - Fakti.bg
articles.summary: From the mountains of Yemen to the regional stage: the rise of the Houthis with the support of Iran  Fakti.bg
articles.full_text:
From a rebel movement in northern Yemen, in two decades the Houthis have become a regional factor capable of threatening global maritime traffic and Saudi Arabia, benefiting from the support of Iran.
Like other armed groups in the region, members of what Tehran calls the "Axis of Resistance", these fighters share an Islamist ideology hostile to the West, summarized in their slogan: "Death to America, Death to Israel". Unlike the Lebanese group "Hezbollah", however, they were not created by the Islamic Republic.
A Coincidence of Interests
"In the beginning, there were no structured ties between Iran and the movement," says Mohammed Azan, a researcher in Islamic thought who witnessed the emergence of the group in Saada, in northern Yemen, in the 1990s. "Their relationship developed gradually, according to the degree to which the two sides discovered common interests," he adds.
Their relationship has strengthened significantly since the war in Gaza and the weakening of the Palestinian movement "Hamas" and other allies of Tehran in the Middle East. But the Houthis are not "a group that follows Iran's orders", emphasizes Maysa Shuja al-Din, a researcher at the Center for Strategic Studies in Sanaa.
Their rapid offensive in September along the Red Sea coast illustrates this alignment of interests.
Control of the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait at a time when Tehran is blocking the Strait of Hormuz on the other side of the Arabian Peninsula, "increases Iran's negotiating power", while giving the Houthis "important leverage" over Riyadh, emphasizes Thomas Junot, a security analyst at the University of Ottawa.
From Saada to the conquest of Yemen
When it was created in 2001, the Houthi movement presented itself as a force representing Saada's interests – the cradle of Zaydism - a distinct branch of Shiism from Iran, whose members had ruled northern Yemen for centuries and were at the time considered marginalized by the central government in Sanaa.
Its founder, Hussein Badreddin al-Houthi, the son of a prominent religious figure, had already denounced Israeli policy and American influence in the Middle East, using rhetoric inspired by Iran's Islamic Revolution.
He was killed by Yemeni authorities in 2004, and the group, later called "Ansar Allah" ("Supporters of God" in Arabic - AFP note.), radicalized under the leadership of his brother Abdel Malik al-Houthi.
Ensconced in the northern mountains, his supporters fought six wars against President Ali Abdullah Saleh before joining the uprising that ousted him in 2012.
In 2014, however, the Houthis allied with him and took power in Sanaa, which was the beginning of their conquest of large parts of Yemen. The former president was assassinated three years later after turning against them.
The intervention of Saudi Arabia, at the head of a military coalition supporting the internationally recognized government in the south of the country, has intensified Iran's interest in the Houthis, although Tehran denies any support for the movement.
The aid is no longer limited to shipments of weapons, but also includes the transfer of knowledge and skills in the field of military affairs, communications and negotiation techniques, says Maysa Shuja al-Din.
Starting from the southern suburbs of Beirut, a Hezbollah stronghold, before settling in Sanaa, the Al-Masirah television channel spreads Houthi propaganda and speeches by their leader, Abdel Malik al-Houthi. Rarely appearing in public, al-Houthi maintains the image of a spiritual leader and defender of the Muslim world against the West and the Gulf states, which he accuses of serving American interests.
"Asymmetric" war
Thanks to their ally Iran, the Houthis have acquired drones and long-range missiles, which has allowed them to establish an "asymmetric balance of power" with Saudi Arabia, notes Thomas Junot.
For years, they have resisted Saudi strikes by "taking advantage of Yemen's geographical features" while at the same time "causing disproportionate damage" to their neighbor by carrying out strikes on its infrastructure.
Since the 2022 ceasefire talks, the movement has strengthened its weapons production capacity and diversified its supply chains – from China to Russia, also using smuggling networks in the Horn of Africa.
According to a report published by the think tank "Century" Foundation in February this year, shipments intercepted for the Houthis between 2021 and 2025 contained mostly weapons-making materials, of which 35 percent originated in China and 21 percent originated in Iran.
"Without Iranian support, the Houthis would not be a regional power today," says Thomas Junot. In Yemen, they have also benefited from the integration of parts of the former national army, from alliances with tribes and, above all, from the "weakness" of the of a government torn by strife and corruption.
This is "a key factor, no less important than Iranian support, in the history of the emergence of the Houthis", summarizes Junot.
(BTA)
(Translated from French: Alexey Margoevsky)
Source: www.bta.bg

articles.title: Iran plans to target Gulf undersea cables if attacked: Report
articles.summary: Iran has prepared detailed plans to strike undersea communications cables in the Gulf in retaliation for any renewed U.S. or Israeli military attack, two senior Iranian security of...
articles.full_text:
Iran has prepared detailed plans to strike undersea communications cables in the Gulf in retaliation for any renewed U.S. or Israeli military attack, two senior Iranian security officials told Reuters, raising concerns over potential disruptions to regional and global connectivity.
Their comments followed warnings by Iranian officials that undersea cables in the region could become targets in any renewed conflict if diplomacy with Washington collapses.
The two Iranian security officials, speaking on condition of anonymity, gave few details and did not say how or where exactly Tehran would carry out such attacks. But one of them said Iran would aim to prevent repairs after any attacks to prolong disruptions to communications, including internet connections.
"If Iran is attacked, there will be no more red lines ... from undersea cables to military bases, including covert ones," one of the officials said.
The official warned Washington not to "play with fire", and said Iran had full access to the undersea cables and could easily destroy them.
Yadollah Javani, the deputy head of political affairs for Iran's Revolutionary Guards (IRGC), said on Wednesday that Iran could target seven major internet cables beneath the Strait of Hormuz if Iranian infrastructure came under attack.
Undersea cables carry around 99% of global internet traffic, according to the International Telecommunication Union, a U.N. agency. But the global impact of such attacks by Iran could be limited as less than 1% of international bandwidth passes through the Strait of Hormuz, said Alan Mauldin, research director at telecommunications research firm TeleGeography.
The strait separates Iran and Oman, linking the Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and Arabian Sea.
The U.S. Department of State and Iran's Foreign Ministry did not respond to Reuters' requests for comment on the Iranian security officials' remarks. There was no immediate comment from Gulf states.
The plans for possible attacks on undersea cables reflect a conviction in Iran's leadership that a renewed US military campaign would have to be met with a stronger response than before.
Top security official Mohsen Rezaei warned this month that US-linked digital infrastructure across the Gulf, including data centres and AI facilities, could be targeted in a renewed conflict.
Washington's Gulf allies have invested heavily in such infrastructure and they "should hold Washington, not Tehran, responsible for any damage to undersea cables," the second Iranian security official said.
Alex Vatanka, director of the Iran program at the Middle East Institute in Washington, said such threats were intended to deter renewed conflict and put pressure on Washington by making Gulf governments and U.S. companies fear for their investments in the region.
"Tehran wants Gulf states and corporate executives to press (U.S. President Donald) Trump over the risks his policies pose to their investment plans," said Vatanka.
Multiple cable cuts could slow internet services and disrupt financial transactions, e-commerce and cloud computing, analysts said. The impact would depend on how operators rerouted traffic and the capacity available on alternative connections, Mauldin said.
Restoring connections during wartime could be difficult, experts said, and higher insurance costs and delays in obtaining permits to enter territorial waters could further complicate repairs.
The Red Sea could offer a more significant target than the Strait of Hormuz, particularly if Iran had support from its Houthi allies in Yemen, though Tehran has made no public statement indicating it plans to target cables there.
The Red Sea carries data between Europe, East Africa and Asia, with capacity routed through it accounting for about 3% of global international demand and around 10% of traffic travelling between regions, Mauldin said.
Gulf governments have been investing heavily in technology to diversify beyond oil and become global artificial intelligence hubs, deepening ties with U.S. technology firms.
Iranian strikes directly hit two Amazon Web Services facilities in the UAE in March and damaged infrastructure near one of its facilities in Bahrain. The IRGC named U.S. tech companies including Microsoft, Google, Apple and Nvidia as legitimate targets at the height of the war in March.
Land-based connections can provide alternative routes for internet traffic, and Gulf states and U.S. technology companies are investing in additional infrastructure to improve resilience.
Microsoft plans to invest more than $400 million in subsea and terrestrial connectivity across the Middle East by 2030.

articles.summary: QatarEnergy Locks Long-Term U.S. LNG Deal  Briefs Finance
articles.full_text:
The deal and the mechanics
QatarEnergy signed a long term purchase agreement on Thursday to take 4 million metric tons of LNG annually from Cheniere Energy through 2054. The price will be indexed to the U.S. Henry Hub benchmark plus a fixed fee, and deliveries are slated to begin in the 2030s.
"We look forward to reliably supplying QatarEnergy from both Sabine Pass and Corpus Christi into the second half of this century," Cheniere CEO Jack Fusco said. On size, Rapidan Energy's Alex Munton called it "about as big as you see in the U.S" for a single deal, even though the volume is less than 1% of a global LNG trade topping 400 million metric tons.
Why the timing matters
Qatar was the second largest LNG exporter behind the U.S. before the war, but shipments have collapsed since Iran bombed the Ras Laffan facility in March. Two production lines were badly damaged, removing roughly 17% of Qatar's LNG capacity for exports. Energy Minister Saad Sherida Al-Kaabi has said repairs will take around three years, and the country has declared force majeure every month since the attack.
"It did give us a big blow, if you will, for our production capability for the next few years," Al-Kaabi said in September. He added that Qatar is exporting "very little" LNG because "we can't export through the Hormuz Strait," noting, "Very sparingly, some ships are crossing the straits but a very small amount, it's not something that would even be measurable in a percentage point."
What happens when Ras Laffan is fixed is still uncertain. Munton said the multidecade Cheniere contract signals Qatar perceives a threat that freedom of navigation in Hormuz "will never return" as Iran continues to attack tankers.

LNG is a seaborne product, he noted, adding, "It's liquefied so it can be put on a ship and that requires access to seaborne routes," and "They've got to access the Strait of Hormuz. There's no other way of getting LNG to market. They're just stuck." With production damaged and Hormuz blocked off, Munton said the Cheniere agreement is a vehicle for QatarEnergy to broaden its LNG trading operations.
Market reaction and wider moves
The Iran war is reshaping flows in a way that benefits U.S. suppliers, cementing American LNG's dominance. Since the war began, shares of Cheniere and Venture Global are up 26% and 40%, respectively. Reuters reported that QatarEnergy is in advanced talks with Venture Global to secure 3 million metric tons per year.
Financing is lining up, too. UBS analyst Manav Gupta said Chinese banks extended a loan of $3 billion earlier this month, which could help QatarEnergy secure additional U.S. LNG to meet delivery commitments. He also said the Cheniere contract challenges the bear case that Cheniere would struggle to add sales and expand capacity.
UBS's price target on Cheniere is $340, implying 18% upside from Thursday's close. Almost 90% of covering analysts assign a buy rating, and their mean target is $314, roughly 9% above Thursday's close.
Views on Venture Global skew positive as well. Close to 60% of analysts call it a buy while the remainder keep it at hold. The consensus price target sits at $17, implying about 35% upside from Thursday's finish. As Munton put it, "The U.S. once again is being called on by buyers to diversify supply," and "so much is under construction in the U.S. that you get to the point where now the U.S. is becoming disproportionately big in terms of global [LNG] market share."
What this could mean for your portfolio
In plain English: long dated contracts are moving toward U.S. LNG while Qatar contends with damaged capacity and a chokepoint at Hormuz. That tilt already shows up in U.S. exporter shares and in sell side targets, with more upside contingent on contract wins and financing. The bottom line: LNG exposure now rides on who can guarantee volumes and shipping lanes for decades.

articles.title: 'Escalation is coming': Middle East on edge as new Israeli-US attack on Iran looms - Middle East Eye
articles.summary: 'Escalation is coming': Middle East on edge as new Israeli-US attack on Iran looms  Middle East Eye
articles.full_text:
US diplomats are preparing for embassy evacuations. Israeli fighter jets are conducting sorties on the Iranian border. The mood among Arab and US officials in the region who spoke to Middle East Eye is that it’s a question of when, not if, the US and Israel resume attacking Iran.
With Iran threatening to retaliate by bombing trillions of dollars worth of US-linked data centres and AI facilities in the Gulf, along with energy installations and airports, the stage seems set for round two of the war.
“An escalation is coming. Whether it’s before the US midterms or after is not relevant. The purpose of the escalation is,” Aaron David Miller, a former Middle East negotiator for Republican and Democratic US presidents, told MEE.
Direct fighting between the US and Iran largely stopped after the signing of a fragile ceasefire in April, but the two never implemented a 14-point Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) signed in June to advance a settlement.
The agreement was widely seen as giving Iran sweeping concessions that experts say the Trump administration simply cannot stomach.
“There is a foundational gap, galactic in scope, that can’t be bridged. The Iranians are not going to change their position on the Strait of Hormuz, the nuclear issue or the Houthis to the extent that Trump needs in order to spin a win,” Miller said.
Trump's emissaries are laying the ground for a return to fighting.
“We are going to have to keep working at this to make sure there’s a regime change eventually,” Republican Senator Rick Scott, a key Trump ally, said in an interview with Fox on Thursday.
Mike Waltz, Trump's ambassador to the United Nations, told The Financial Times that the White House is ready for a prolonged conflict.
"The president and the US Navy can maintain this blockade [on Iranian ports] for the foreseeable future,” he said in an interview released on Friday.
A war that started over what the US claimed to be strikes aimed at crippling Iran’s nuclear programme has drifted into an all-encompassing battle over who calls the shots in the Middle East.
For example, Iran wants to impose fees on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz. Iran and the US have conducted tit-for-tat strikes in the waterway. The US has imposed a blockade against Iran that is devastating its economy, while Iran is attacking vessels there, sending shipping rates soaring.
At least 27 ships have been attacked this month alone, the highest number since March.
The tensions between the two have also contributed to the collapse of a ceasefire in Yemen, where fighting between the Iran-aligned Houthis and Saudi-backed internationally recognised government is raging.
Experts say a return to war may be inevitable because the status quo suits neither the Trump administration nor Tehran, but neither side feels weak enough to make concessions.
'US watches oil volumes, Iran watches the price'
Iran and Trump are both watching the oil market and gleaning different lessons from it, Gregory Brew, an expert on energy and Iran at Eurasia Group, a geopolitical consultancy, told MEE.
This week, energy firm Kpler published data showing that Middle East oil and product exports reached pre-Iran war levels last week. Some experts cautioned that the data is skewed towards a burst in activity, but more oil is coming out of the region from US allies, while Iran’s exports are choked by the US blockade.
Saudi Arabia is exporting oil via the Red Sea, bypassing the Houthis, who control the Bab al-Mandab, with a pipeline to the Mediterranean. Meanwhile, Gulf states inside the Strait of Hormuz are using a shuttle service by which state-owned boats bring oil to larger tankers waiting in the Gulf of Oman. The US says its navy is escorting the vessels, but at a high cost.
The rise in volumes has not lowered the price. Brent, the international benchmark, is up a whopping 43 percent since the MoU was signed with Iran. Diesel prices are up around 35 percent, while gasoline is up less than 10 percent.
No one doubts that Iran’s economy is hurting. Inflation in September was up a staggering 90 percent, but Brew said that Iran’s rulers believe they can endure another round of fighting while the Trump administration will fold.
“If the US is watching volumes in Hormuz, the Iranians are watching price. And they are pretty confident they can withstand pressure over a longer period of time than Trump can,” Brew, at Eurasia Group, said.
“In a context where the US and Israel are bombing Iran again directly, we are certain to see more aggressive Iranian strikes on energy infrastructure. The US will also have fewer resources to manage this escort system,” he said.
"Energy prices will stay elevated," he added.
'Devastating for the Gulf'
Before the US and Israel attacked Iran in February, there was a lobbying dash from some Gulf states to stop it. During the war, Saudi Arabia and the UAE joined the US in striking Iran, but then Riyadh pivoted to supporting mediation. Reuters reported that the UAE paid Iran to stop attacking it.
In round two, experts say, the Gulf will struggle to remain strategically relevant, although it will be on the front lines of Iran’s reprisals. The Gulf states faced thousands of drone and missile attacks from Iran after the US and Israel’s February attack.
“From the Gulf perspective, this is going to be devastating,” Abdullah Baabood, an Omani academic and international relations expert, said. “Already we see serious economic problems in the Gulf.”
Asharq Bloomberg reported Bahrain is expected to receive a bailout led by the UAE to shore up its collapsing foreign currency reserves. Qatar’s economy shrank 15 percent year-on-year. The IMF expects the UAE’s economy to shrink four percent. Saudi Arabia has had to cancel a prominent investment conference because of Houthi attacks.
“The Gulf is hostage to a crisis that has no end,” Baabood said. “Qatar is trying to mediate. Oman has been pushed aside by Trump. The UAE, Kuwait and Saudi Arabia are very quiet. They just don’t know what to do. They can’t read Trump.”
“Other than Israel, no one has real interest in a serious continuation of the war,” Marwan Muasher, a former Jordanian foreign minister and vice president for studies at Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, told MEE.
The expectations of a return to war come against the backdrop of Israeli general elections next week. In his endorsement of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Trump raised the stakes of fresh strikes, saying he wanted help to “finish the job” against Iran “unless they change their ways rapidly”.
Experts say that given the war’s popularity in Israel, a return to fighting could help Netanyahu before the vote, or help him stay on as prime minister if the outcome of elections is indecisive.
Baabood said that no one doubts Israel and the US’s ability to “devastate” Iran’s infrastructure, but that the Islamic Republic can still do “significant” damage to the Gulf.
In an interview with Dropsite News this week, Major General Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, left little doubt that Iran would attack Gulf energy sites if the US resumes the war.
“If the US strategy is to prolong the war while using neighbouring countries’ energy infrastructure to offset the pressure arising from Hormuz and maintain the blockade of Iran, those governments should not assume they can participate in economic warfare against Iran without putting themselves at risk,” he said.
Where is the pain for Donald Trump?
One of the key questions in a second round of fighting is how well the Gulf states can defend against Iranian attacks that may spike energy prices further.
A US Inspector General’s report in September said that the US faces "strategic inventory shortfalls” in key munitions. MEE reported in March that the US was already short of interceptors. That was before weeks of high-intensity fighting in the region. The Trump administration has repeatedly denied being short of munitions.
The Gulf states' vulnerability to Iranian drones has been crystallised by strikes from the Houthis on Saudi Arabia in recent weeks.
The kingdom is reeling under the weight of Houthi attacks which have repeatedly targeted its airports and high-profile energy sites. At least 21 people have been killed in Houthi attacks on Saudi airports since the start of October, including religious pilgrims, according to the kingdom’s authorities. An attack attributed to militias in Iraq aligned with Iran hit the kingdom’s East-West Pipeline in September.
"Continuing the war will only bring more difficulties to countries in the Gulf, and it’s clear it will not result in regime change in Iran. Meanwhile, Trump is suffering domestically because of rising fuel and food prices” in the US, Muasher told MEE.
But Miller, now a senior fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, said that Trump may feel less restraint than he is given credit for, particularly given his anger at Iran for stymying his plans for a quick victory earlier this year.
“There is no cost-benefit analysis because Donald Trump is going to be OK. He may lose the House and maybe the Senate in midterms, but he will be OK. His family will be OK. He will build his presidential library,” Miller said.
“Trump's urgency to end this thing is not evident. There is no accountability. Where is the pain for Donald Trump?”

Welcome To ChemAnalyst
	Cheniere Energy has secured a major long-term liquefied natural gas (LNG) supply agreement with QatarEnergy, committing to deliver a combined 4 million tonnes per annum (MTPA) of LNG through the end of 2054. The deal strengthens the position of US LNG in global energy markets and reinforces long-term commercial ties between two major players in the international gas industry.
	Under the agreements, subsidiaries Sabine Pass Liquefaction LLC and Corpus Christi Liquefaction LLC will each supply QatarEnergy with 2 MTPA of LNG. The contracts are structured on a free-on-board (FOB) basis, with prices linked to the US Henry Hub natural gas benchmark plus a fixed fee. Deliveries are scheduled to begin in the early 2030s and continue for more than two decades, extending into the second half of the century.
	However, 1 MTPA of the volume contracted through Sabine Pass remains conditional on a positive final investment decision for the first phase of the facility's expansion project.
	Cheniere Chairman, President and Chief Executive Officer Jack Fusco described the agreements as a significant multi-decade commercial commitment. He highlighted the company's operational reliability, established customer relationships and experience in supplying international LNG markets as key factors supporting the deal. The agreements also reinforce Cheniere's ambitions to maintain its position as a leading US LNG exporter.
	Sabine Pass Expansion to Boost Capacity
	The agreements are also significant for Cheniere's planned expansion of its Sabine Pass Liquefaction Project in Louisiana. Through Cheniere Energy Partners, the company is developing an expansion designed to add peak production capacity of up to approximately 20 MTPA, including estimated debottlenecking opportunities. The expansion could increase the facility's total production capacity to more than 50 MTPA.

articles.title: Are global oil reserves sufficient to withstand renewed US-Iran war? - Al Jazeera
articles.summary: Are global oil reserves sufficient to withstand renewed US-Iran war?  Al Jazeera
articles.full_text:
Oil prices have climbed towards their highest levels in five months as attacks on tankers in and around the Strait of Hormuz mount and efforts to end the United States-Israel war on Iran are deadlocked.
Brent crude, the international benchmark, rose by more than $2 to $110.85 a barrel on Wednesday, close to a five-month peak.
A day earlier, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said two tankers were “set ablaze” after hitting mines at what it called an illegal crossing point in the strait. Then, on Thursday, the IRGC said it hit seven more tankers although Washington dismissed the claim. In a statement, the IRGC said four of the vessels were transferring oil when they were targeted and caught fire overnight.
In September, the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), seized territory in Yemen close to the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a critical chokepoint into and out of the Red Sea and a gateway to Egypt’s Suez Canal.
The escalation came as the world’s emergency oil stocks, already tapped heavily since the Iran war began on February 28, sit at their lowest levels in decades.
Al Jazeera put a question to analysts: If fighting resumes in full, the Strait of Hormuz is shut off completely and Houthi attacks choke off Bab al-Mandeb, how long could the world’s reserves last?
Here’s what you need to know:
What emergency oil reserves are there?
Strategic oil reserves are stockpiles of crude oil and fuel held by governments or by companies on their behalf for use in a supply emergency.
The International Energy Agency (IEA), which was established in 1974 after the Arab oil embargo, coordinates most of them. Its importing members must hold at least 90 days of net imports. China and India are not members.
How much of the reserves has already been released this year?
A record amount.
On March 11, days after the start of the US-Israel war on Iran, the IEA’s 32 members agreed to make 400 million barrels available from emergency supplies, more than double the volume released after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
The US pledged 172.2 million barrels from its Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) and Japan 79.8 million, according to IEA figures.
The SPR has since fallen to 283 million barrels, its lowest level since October 1982, according to the US Department of Energy.
Much of that oil was lent rather than sold and must be returned with extra barrels, according to the US Energy Information Administration.
How much oil is left?
Far less than before the war began in February, and not all of it can be used.
Aaron Kildow, a senior crude oil analyst at Sparta Commodities, told Al Jazeera that global strategic stocks excluding China and Iran have fallen by nearly 327 million barrels since the end of December 2025 with the US, Europe and Japan accounting for about 95 percent of the draw.
He estimated that leaves only about 400 million barrels of usable reserves worldwide, excluding China’s stockpile, which is unlikely to be exported, and Gulf stocks, which could be cut off by a total closure of Hormuz.
Nearly half of these available stocks are in Japan.
Europe has about 76 million barrels uncommitted, but members such as Germany are holding some back for a local emergency, Kildow said.
“Europe is the real wildcard, both on timing and willingness,” Kildow said.
Meanwhile, China’s onshore crude stocks stand at 1.13 billion barrels, down from 1.23 billion in late February but still enough for about 80 days of refinery intake, Muyu Xu, a senior crude oil analyst at the analytics firm Kpler, told Al Jazeera.
India’s reserves cover just eight days of its imports, the Reuters news agency reported.
What would a full closure of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb mean?
Before the war, about one-fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas supplies, or roughly 20 million barrels of oil a day, passed through the Strait of Hormuz.
Saudi Arabia has increased the amount of crude it transports from its oilfields in the east to its Red Sea port of Yanbu in the west via the East-West Pipeline, thereby bypassing Hormuz.
But there have been strikes on that pipeline, and tankers heading south from Yanbu must pass through Bab a-Mandeb, where the Iran-backed Houthis declared a blockade on Saudi shipping in July.
Only a confirmed 373,000 barrels a day of Saudi crude have transited Bab al-Mandeb so far this month, the lowest level since February, Xu said, with most Yanbu cargoes now heading north via Egypt instead.
If Hormuz were shut and the Houthis blocked all Saudi tankers, Gulf producers could export only through a few pipelines and Yanbu’s northbound route, Xu said.
That would leave about 7.5 million barrels a day of Middle Eastern crude, against 16.8 million now, a shortfall of about 9.3 million barrels a day, she estimated.
“If such attacks occur, the supply disruption could be even more severe and prolonged,” Xu said, referring to strikes on oilfields, terminals and pipelines.
So how long would reserves last?
Not for long – possibly just weeks, according to experts.
If Kpler’s estimated shortfall had to be covered entirely from the roughly 400 million usable barrels that Kildow identified, they could not, in practice, be released that fast. Japanese and South Korean reserves can move quickly, Kildow said, but US barrels are staged over three months, and Europe’s contribution is uncertain.
Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at IG Group, said the world was fortunate after the first closure. “The salient feature of March and beyond was how a crisis didn’t actually develop. We got away with it,” he said.
“I don’t think the global economy will be as lucky next time if there is a protracted conflict,” Beauchamp said. “A month or two is all we have.”
The world would not literally run out of oil. Instead, prices would rise until enough demand disappeared. “One hundred fifty dollars [per barrel] becomes a very distinct possibility, which then sees significant demand destruction,” Beauchamp said.
The sharpest squeeze would be on diesel, which is already nearly double the price of crude, the IEA said.
Refiners would compete for crude grades rich in diesel, “a cost that ultimately lands on consumers,” Kildow said.
Who would feel it first?
Asian importers with thin reserves.
Most Gulf exports in September and October went to Asian buyers, and India and Pakistan are among the most exposed, Kildow said, adding that their nearest alternative supply, from West Africa, is 25 to 28 days away by sea, compared with two days from Fujairah in the United Arab Emirates.
“The squeeze won’t hit uniformly. It lands fastest and hardest where reserves are thinnest and substitute supply is farthest away,” Kildow said.
Who would gain?
Oil producers far from the Gulf.
In the second quarter of this year, as the US-Iran war was under way, ExxonMobil reported earnings of $14.5bn, its highest in four years while Chevron posted $12bn, its best in six years and Shell more than doubled its earnings to nearly $10bn. Their profits are largely down to the high oil prices.
A second shock would send refiners scrambling for supplies from the US, Latin America, West Africa and Russia, Xu said.
“This would allow non-Middle Eastern producers to benefit from higher crude prices, potentially alongside lower transportation costs,” she said.
In August, US President Donald Trump said companies such as ExxonMobil and Chevron were “making too much money based on a shortage”.

articles.title: The world is once again on the edge: Hormuz and the Red Sea — Phar Kim Beng - Malay Mail
articles.summary: The world is once again on the edge: Hormuz and the Red Sea — Phar Kim Beng  Malay Mail
articles.full_text:
OCTOBER 24 — The world is once again approaching a dangerous strategic precipice.
This time, the epicentre of instability lies in two of the most important maritime arteries of international commerce: the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea.
The consequences of their simultaneous disruption cannot be overstated.
What is unfolding is no longer merely a confrontation between Iran, Israel and the United States.
It is becoming a systemic threat to global economic stability, energy security and international peace.
The unprecedented meeting of eight European and Middle Eastern foreign ministers in Istanbul on October 23, 2026, is therefore significant. Britain, France, Germany and Italy joined Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Egypt in an attempt to prevent further military escalation.
Their message was unmistakable. Diplomacy must prevail over military adventurism.
The reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and the restoration of maritime security in the Red Sea are essential to preventing an already dangerous regional conflict from becoming a wider international catastrophe.
Yet the very necessity of such a meeting reveals how precarious the international situation has become.
The Strait of Hormuz is not an ordinary maritime passage. Approximately one-fifth of global oil consumption is transported through this narrow waterway between Iran and Oman.
Any prolonged disruption immediately affects energy prices, shipping insurance, industrial production and the cost of living across continents.
The Red Sea is equally consequential. Together with the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and the Suez Canal, it connects Asian manufacturing centres with European markets.
When both maritime corridors become insecure simultaneously, the global economy faces a double strategic shock.
Oil and liquefied natural gas become more expensive. Commercial vessels must consider longer and costlier routes. Freight charges increase.
Supply chains become unpredictable.
Eventually, these costs are transmitted to ordinary households through higher prices for food, transportation, electricity and manufactured goods.
This is precisely why the crisis cannot be treated as a distant Middle Eastern confrontation.
For Malaysia and Asean, the dangers are immediate.
South-east Asia remains deeply integrated into global maritime commerce.
The region’s manufacturing industries, electronics exports, energy imports and food supply chains depend on predictable international shipping.
Although Malaysia is an important energy producer, it is not insulated from volatility in global oil and gas markets.
Higher energy prices may benefit certain exporters temporarily, but they also impose substantial costs on industries, consumers and governments.
Malaysia’s fiscal calculations under Budget 2027 could become increasingly difficult if international energy prices remain elevated while shipping disruptions generate additional inflationary pressures.
Nor can Asean assume that its strategic distance from West Asia guarantees economic security.
The Strait of Malacca, South China Sea, Indian Ocean and Red Sea form interconnected segments of a global maritime system.
Instability in one corridor inevitably affects commercial calculations in another.
Indeed, the present crisis demonstrates the limitations of viewing maritime security exclusively through the narrow prism of territorial sovereignty.
Maritime chokepoints are international economic lifelines. Their disruption produces consequences far beyond the states immediately surrounding them.
The attacks by Yemen’s Houthis against Saudi Arabia and commercial shipping have further complicated this strategic landscape.
Saudi Arabia is not merely another regional power.
It is one of the world’s most consequential energy producers and a central pillar of economic stability in the Gulf.
Repeated attacks against Saudi infrastructure, airports and maritime facilities threaten to transform an already volatile situation into a sustained regional emergency.
The Houthis must therefore cease attacks against civilian infrastructure and international shipping.
However, the military containment of the Houthis cannot become a substitute for a comprehensive political settlement in Yemen.
Nor should the United States and Israel assume that renewed attacks against Iran will automatically produce strategic stability.
Quite the contrary.
Further strikes against Iran could provoke retaliation against energy facilities, military installations and commercial vessels across the Gulf.
A cycle of attack and counterattack would be particularly dangerous because the geographical boundaries of the conflict are becoming increasingly blurred.
Iran possesses various means of imposing costs on its adversaries, while its regional relationships and associated armed groups create additional risks of escalation.
At the same time, Iran must recognise that restricting international navigation through Hormuz undermines the interests of countries that are not parties to the conflict.
The freedom of navigation cannot become a bargaining chip in an escalating military confrontation.
The Istanbul meeting is especially important because Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan have already established the Mecca Defence Alliance.
This emerging arrangement demonstrates that regional powers are increasingly determined to assume greater responsibility for their own security.
Yet collective defence and collective escalation are not synonymous.
The Mecca Defence Alliance must function as a deterrent against aggression rather than an instrument for widening the war.
Turkey’s diplomatic experience, Saudi Arabia’s economic significance and Pakistan’s military capabilities could provide an important foundation for regional stability.
Egypt, meanwhile, occupies a strategically indispensable position because of its relationship with the Suez Canal and the Red Sea.
Its participation strengthens the possibility of a regional security framework that does not depend exclusively on American military power.
European participation adds another layer of significance.
France, Germany, Britain and Italy understand that instability in Hormuz and the Red Sea will eventually undermine European economic recovery, energy security and industrial competitiveness.
Their presence in Istanbul suggests a growing recognition that military pressure alone cannot resolve the Iranian crisis.
The emerging diplomatic consensus should therefore be translated into concrete measures: an immediate reduction in hostilities, protection of civilian infrastructure, restoration of safe maritime passage and sustained negotiations involving the principal regional actors.
For Malaysia, the implications extend beyond economics.
As a maritime trading nation and a member of Asean, Malaysia has every reason to support diplomatic initiatives that prevent further fragmentation of the international order.
Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s government should continue advocating restraint, respect for international law and negotiated settlements.
Malaysia should also strengthen consultations with Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Egypt, Pakistan and its Asean partners on the economic and strategic implications of the crisis.
Asean’s own experience with dialogue, confidence-building measures and inclusive regional institutions provides useful lessons.
The Asean Regional Forum, East Asia Summit and Asean Defence Ministers’ Meeting-Plus demonstrate that adversarial powers can remain engaged even when their strategic interests diverge.
Such mechanisms do not eliminate conflict. They reduce the possibility that misunderstanding, miscalculation or political overconfidence will turn a manageable confrontation into a catastrophe.
The world is already confronting multiple overlapping crises, from the Russia-Ukraine war to persistent tensions in the Indo-Pacific.
Adding a prolonged confrontation across Hormuz and the Red Sea would deepen the fragmentation of global commerce and accelerate the erosion of international confidence.
The Istanbul initiative must therefore be judged not by the number of foreign ministers assembled, but by its ability to prevent further escalation.
There is no strategic wisdom in allowing the world’s principal energy and commercial arteries to become permanent theatres of military confrontation.
The international community must recognise that the costs of another round of escalation will not be borne exclusively by Iran, Israel, Saudi Arabia or the United States.
They will be distributed across the entire world, particularly among developing economies already struggling with inflation, debt and fiscal constraints.
The choice is increasingly stark.
Either the principal powers exercise strategic restraint and restore the primacy of diplomacy, or the world risks entering another prolonged period of economic turbulence and geopolitical disorder.
Hormuz and the Red Sea must remain corridors of international commerce, not become the fault lines of a wider war.
The world is already dangerously close to the edge. Another reckless military escalation could push it beyond the point where diplomacy can easily restore stability.
* Phar Kim Beng, PhD is the Professor of Asean Studies at International Islamic University of Malaysia and Director of Institute of International and Asean Studies (IINTAS).

articles.title: [不同来源] China Uses Djibouti Outpost to Assert Itself on Houthi Attacks - Breitbart
articles.summary: China Uses Djibouti Outpost to Assert Itself on Houthi Attacks  Breitbart
articles.full_text:
China and Djibouti released a joint communique on Thursday supporting freedom of navigation in the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which are currently under threat from the Iran-backed Houthi insurgents of Yemen.
The statement was issued after Djibouti’s Foreign Minister Abdoulkader Houssein Omar met with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi in Beijing.
“The two sides emphasised the importance of safeguarding freedom of navigation in the Red Sea and the Bab al-Mandeb Strait and stressed that the navigation rights exercised by merchant vessels of all countries in accordance with international law should be respected,” the communique said.
“China supports Red Sea coastal states in constructively safeguarding the unobstructed and secure operation of international shipping lanes and protecting the region’s common interests,” it added.
Djibouti is a small state across the Bab el-Mandeb Strait from Yemen. China’s only acknowledged overseas naval base was established in Djibouti ten years ago and was recently upgraded with enhanced intelligence-gathering capabilities.
The People’s Republic of China (PRC) has become the top foreign investor in Djibouti, pumping money into port facilities, railroads, and gas pipelines as part of China’s Belt and Road Initiative (BRI). As usual with BRI client states, Djibouti has accumulated enormous debt to Chinese banks, which gives Beijing a great deal of leverage over the small Horn of Africa state.
U.S. officials have grown increasingly wary of China’s presence in Djibouti, as the Chinese naval base sits along one of the world’s busiest shipping lanes, and the People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) base in Djibouti is less than ten miles away from Camp Lemonnier, the primary base of operations for the U.S. Africa Command (AFRICOM) in the Horn of Africa.
China certainly has strong reasons to want safe passage for commercial vessels through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, with some $120 billion in imports to China and $160 billion in exports flowing through Red Sea shipping routes. China would suffer as much as any other oil buyer, and perhaps more, if Houthi terrorism shut down the alternative Red Sea oil flows that were created to work around the Strait of Hormuz.
The Diplomat found the China-Djibouti communique disappointing, a symbolic expression of concern stuffed with generic demands for “all parties” to commit to “easing tensions” that was mostly of interest as China’s first joint statement with a Red Sea nation.
The only potential threat to Red Sea shipping is the Houthis, who waged a campaign of piracy during the Gaza War and have threatened to do it again, so mumbling about “all parties” will only encourage the Houthis to think they would be rewarded with concessions for further terrorism.
“The Horn of Africa must never be used as a geopolitical arena, and the flames of war in the Middle East must never be brought to the Horn of Africa,” the China-Djibouti statement said. Only Iran and its Houthi proxies are threatening to do that, and China offered no clue as to how it might snuff those “flames of war” if the Houthis decide to ignite them.
“During their talks, Wang told Omar that China will ‘support’ Djibouti ‘in building itself into a regional hub for trade, logistics, and connectivity.’ But Djibouti’s ambitions — and China’s billions in investments — have little hope if the Red Sea is closed to shipping by militant attacks,” The Diplomat noted.
The South China Morning Post (SCMP) on Thursday quoted “Chinese analysts” who said “the situation in the Red Sea had not yet escalated to a level that warranted direct naval escorts, though Beijing would closely monitor the region and might take action if the country’s shipping came under threat.”

articles.title: If you think the Houthis are just a Saudi problem, think again - Arab News
articles.summary: If you think the Houthis are just a Saudi problem, think again  Arab News
articles.full_text:
Saudi Arabia may now be bearing the brunt of Houthi attacks that have sought to murder civilians at its airports, cripple its critical energy infrastructure, and demolish its military installations. But make no mistake, Saudi Arabia is only the Houthis’ most immediate grievance. They have the potential — and arguably the inclination — to do much worse. Their slogan, “God is Great, Death to America, Death to Israel, Cursed are the Jews, Victory to Islam,” should not be read as a rhetorical flourish. The Houthis, who have a long history of belligerence toward the US and the West generally, are literally telling us what they plan to do.
The Houthis began as a regional insurgency in northern Yemen in the early 2000s, but by 2014, they occupied swaths of Yemeni territory, swept into the capital Sanaa, and took control of many government institutions. Shortly afterward, Saudi Arabia began a military campaign to remove them from power and destroy their leadership. Under pressure from the US, the Saudis eventually sought to de-escalate the conflict and pursue diplomacy.
In late 2023, however, ostensibly in response to Israel’s war on Gaza and in solidarity with Hamas after its Oct. 7 assault on Israel, the Houthis began attacking commercial shipping in the Red Sea and targeting US naval vessels. There were credible reports that they were conniving with Russia, which was giving them intelligence — payback for US support for Ukraine, we assumed — and China, which was shipping the Houthis parts for their home-made drones and ballistic missiles. Although the Houthis cast their attacks as retribution for the Gaza war, I was in Riyadh in that period serving as US ambassador, and we had little expectation that it would all blow over whenever the Gaza war ended.
The Houthis are widely regarded as a proxy of Iran, but ending the current war with Iran — like ending the Gaza conflict — will not stop the Houthis. Yes, they welcome Iranian military and financial support. But they do not regard themselves as Iran’s agents. Rather, they actually see their movement on par with Iran, essentially their own Islamic Republic, except with such an exaggerated belief in their own religious legitimacy that they set their sights on controlling not just Yemeni territory, but the holy — Saudi — cities of Makkah and Madinah. That political distance between Iran and the Houthis is dangerous because it means that an eventual deal with Iran is not necessarily binding on the Houthis.
The US should start planning with its partners now with the express goal of eventually eliminating the Houthis’ ability to wreak terror in Yemen and beyond
Michael Ratney
There is a view, certainly plausible, that the Houthis are not like other insurgencies or terrorist organizations. Unlike Hamas or Hezbollah, which have systems for regenerating leadership, the Houthis are more like a cult, beholden to their leader, Abdulmalek Al-Houthi, who has few potential replacements. In 2024, the Biden administration embarked on a concerted effort to degrade the Houthis’ capacity to threaten their neighbors. I believe it could have been successful, especially if we had brought additional partners into the fight. The Trump administration continued that effort until May 2025, but suspended it after reportedly striking a ceasefire deal which only required that the Houthis stop targeting US ships — in other words with no commitment to stop targeting others. The agreement was apparently struck without consulting either Saudi Arabia or Israel, then the two countries most directly threatened by Houthi drones and ballistic missiles.
We should be clear about ceasefires with the Houthis: Their leaders are ideologues, not pragmatists, and they will constantly look for pretexts to escalate. That happened in July 2026 when Houthi missiles — then mostly intercepted — began targeting Saudi Arabia after the Kingdom refused to allow the Houthis to establish an uninspected air corridor between Sanaa and Tehran that would have violated UN Security Council sanctions. The Houthis then announced a blockade of ships carrying Saudi crude oil through the Bab Al-Mandab, and began attacking Saudi energy infrastructure, military targets, and airports. Fighting then escalated between Saudi-backed forces in Yemen and the Houthis. On Oct. 10, a Houthi projectile targeting the Riyadh airport hit a terminal, killing more than a dozen people and injuring over 300, including pilgrims of multiple nationalities on their way to Makkah.
The current explosion of violence came as the Yemeni armed forces, with support from Saudi Arabia, sought to push back recent Houthi gains around the Bab Al-Mandab, the strategic waterway at the mouth of the Red Sea. About 25 percent of global container traffic normally passes through that waterway — another reminder that the Houthis are not just a Saudi problem.
Sooner or later, the US and others in the international community are going to have to get involved beyond the non-kinetic support now reportedly being offered. This might not be today, at a time when the US military arsenal may be depleted, and the calamitous conflict with Iran may not yet be over. But looking ahead it will simply be untenable to leave in place the Houthis, an organization that brazenly threatens our allies, conspires with our adversaries, targets our navy, inflates global shipping costs, terrorizes mariners, depresses the region’s economy, pollutes the Red Sea, kidnaps the Yemeni employees of our former embassy in Sanaa as well as UN employees, and aims to cement its violent control over one of the world’s most impoverished populations — and over one of the world’s most strategic waterways.
The US should start planning with its partners now with the express goal of eventually eliminating the Houthis’ ability to wreak terror in Yemen and beyond.
- Michael Ratney is the former US ambassador to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.

articles.title: OPEC Fund issues $250M for Middle Corridor's missing railway section in Türkiye - Trend News Agency
articles.summary: OPEC Fund issues $250M for Middle Corridor's missing railway section in Türkiye  Trend News Agency
articles.full_text:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 23. OPEC Fund has allocated $250 million for the missing railway section of the Middle Corridor in Türkiye.
This was announced in a report published on the OPEC page.
According to the information, the OPEC Fund has joined a large-scale international initiative to eliminate the missing link in railway communication between Asia and Europe.
“A loan of $250 million will be used to build a new 127-kilometer railway line, which will bypass the Istanbul metropolitan area and provide high-capacity rail links across the Bosphorus.
It is the largest single financing in the institution’s history and forms part of an approved package of up to $500 million. The project will address a key infrastructure gap on three international trade routes passing through Istanbul and served by rail: the Trans-Caspian Middle Corridor, connecting China and Central Asia with Europe; the Iraq Development Road corridor, which will link Asia and the European Union through the Middle East and Türkiye through rail links; the Türkiye-EU corridor, which accounts for a third of Türkiye's international trade," OPEC said.
According to the report, the project will redirect part of the cargo transportation from road to electrified rail transport with lower carbon emissions, and will also strengthen Türkiye’s position as a logistics hub connecting Europe, Asia, and the Middle East.
“The total investment of $8.3 billion is being provided by an international group of sponsors led and administered by the World Bank. They include the Asian Development Bank, the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, the Islamic Development Bank, the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development and the European Investment Bank, alongside the Government of Türkiye.
Istanbul is one of the largest cities in the world, located on two continents. Currently, rail traffic across the Bosphorus Strait is carried out through the Marmaray tunnel, which was built primarily for passenger traffic. Freight trains can only use the tunnel during limited nighttime hours, keeping rail freight capacity through the strait to about 3 million tons a year.
To address this limitation, a new 127-kilometer electrified rail corridor will be built between Çayırova on the Asian side and Çatalca on the European side. The crossing of the Bosphorus will be carried out via the Yavuz Sultan Selim Bridge, also known as the Third Bridge," OPEC noted.
The report pointed out that the new line will be double-track, electrified, equipped with a full-fledged signaling system, and designed for both passenger and freight traffic.
“Thanks to the project, the annual capacity of rail freight traffic across the Bosphorus will increase to 50 million tons.
It will carry both passengers and freight, and will connect Istanbul Airport and Sabiha Gökçen Airport and the national rail network.
Freight journey times between Çayırova and Çatalca will fall from around 13 hours to 3.6 hours. Travel by public transport between the two airports will drop from approximately two hours to 65 minutes.
The OPEC Fund signed its first loan agreement with Türkiye in 1979. It has since approved almost $850 million for transport infrastructure, agriculture, health, energy and other sectors, including recent loans addressing food security and climate resilience,” the report added.
The Middle Corridor is a multimodal trade and transport route connecting Asia and Europe through Central Asia, the Caspian Sea, Azerbaijan, Georgia, and Türkiye. The route begins in China and runs through Central Asia before crossing the Caspian Sea and continuing through Azerbaijan, Georgia, and Türkiye to European markets.
The Middle Corridor is being developed as an alternative to traditional northern and southern transport routes, providing connectivity between Asian markets, including China, and Europe.

A U.S. envoy warned Friday that Washington could launch military strikes against Iran as early as this weekend, raising fears of a renewed confrontation amid escalating threats from the U.S. and Israel.
"Could there be a strike this weekend? Absolutely," Tom Barrack, the U.S. ambassador to Türkiye and point man on Syria who does not have a direct role on Iran, told podcast host Mario Nawfal.
President Donald Trump "is very clear. He's open and available and accessible to a deal and we've been at the table for months and months and months," Barrack said in an interview as he visited the Gulf.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who faces elections Tuesday, has in recent days repeatedly vowed to topple the regime in Iran, following two major bombing campaigns against it since last year.
Trump has also signalled an openness to resuming strikes after a long deadlock in diplomacy, although he earlier said it would not happen before US congressional elections on November 3.
Barrack, in remarks that contradict Netanyahu, said the U.S. was not looking to topple the regime, a sworn enemy of the United States and Israel since a 1979 revolution toppled the shah.
"If you keep threatening the world, our allies, the Gulf, there will be a consequence. The consequence won't be regime change," Barrack said.
"The United States -- the president of the United States -- has said he's not interested in regime change," he added.
"The problem with regime change always is, what's the day-two scenario?"

Speaking to Gulf Times on the sidelines of the Global Security Forum, Antonino Maggiore said the two sides are working to translate their shared interests into concrete initiatives, with negotiations on a strategic partnership agreement providing a framework for closer engagement.
“We need to structure our co-operation,” he said.“We need to operationalise this co-operation because, as I said, it's based on a convergence of principles. With principles, we need implementation.”
One forthcoming initiative is an EU-Gulf Co-operation Council (GCC) seminar on defence technology and AI, scheduled for Doha on December 3.
The event aims to bring defence industries from the EU's 27 member states together with their Qatari counterparts and representatives from across the Gulf.
Maggiore said the EU could provide a platform for industries from its member states to interact with partners in Qatar and the wider region.
“These fields, security and defence and AI technology, are important in the partnership with Qatar,” he said, describing the seminar as part of efforts to develop cooperation in areas of growing strategic importance.
The initiative comes amid wider discussions on how Qatar and the EU can respond to changing security challenges, strengthen technological capabilities and establish practical channels for collaboration.
Asked about Qatar's growing role in international diplomacy and mediation, Maggiore lauded the country's contribution to efforts to address regional crises and other international issues.
“We commend, allow me to say, very, very much the prominent role of Qatar in mediation, also in the ongoing crisis in the region, but on so many other dossiers and so many other tables where Qatar is showing to be a global player of mediation and diplomacy,” he said.
He pointed to the Doha Forum in December as another opportunity to demonstrate Qatar's diplomatic role, adding that the EU wanted to strengthen co-operation on mediation, maritime security, respect for international law and security.
The ambassador said the strategic partnership agreement under negotiation with Qatar would help organise co-operation across these areas, alongside separate initiatives designed to deliver tangible outcomes.
Economic engagement is another priority, particularly support for small- and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), investment and start-ups.
During a media Q&A session, Maggiore outlined plans for a council that would bring together chambers of commerce from EU member states, corresponding Qatari entities, and European institutions.
A second component would build on the existing European Enterprise Network, which connects European businesses and SMEs and works with partners in non-EU countries.
“We want to support exchanges, investments, start-ups, youth,” he said.“Both big investments and also to SMEs. SMEs are cornerstones of the European Union.”
He said smaller businesses could benefit from structured support and connections that larger multinational companies often already have, adding that the EU saw considerable potential for closer economic ties with Qatar.
Trade is also part of the strategic partnership agreement discussions with Qatar and at the GCC level.
Energy remains central to the relationship.
Maggiore said he recently met Qatar's minister of state for energy and stressed that dialogue on energy co-operation continues with the European Commission and EU member states.
He described Qatar's liquefied natural gas (LNG) as being of“strategic importance for the EU”, adding that Brussels is fully aware of its significance.
Maggiore also praised Qatar's engagement to maintain supplies and avoid unnecessary disruption, acknowledging the impact of the regional situation on production facilities.
“We are very pleased that Qatar is doing everything that is possible to maintain its engagement,” he said.
People-to-people ties and mobility are another area under discussion, the envoy said, with the EU working towards possible visa liberalisation for Qatari nationals.
Maggiore said the postponement of the EU-GCC summit, originally scheduled for October 24, would not affect the momentum of discussions on visas or the wider strategic partnership.
“The work is ongoing with, I would say, priority from our side,” he said, adding that meetings were taking place in Brussels with GCC countries and EU member states, which are responsible for issuing visas.“This is a priority for us, and it's something we are working on very intensively.”
On the wider regional situation, Maggiore said that the Gulf and Europe shared concerns about instability and the threat of escalation.
He reiterated the EU's support for dialogue, de-escalation, international law and a two-state solution to the Palestinian question.
The envoy also reaffirmed the EU's opposition to illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank.
He highlighted its humanitarian assistance to Palestine, while acknowledging that differences among member states could complicate the development of a common position.
Maggiore said the EU is ready to play a role in initiatives aimed at stabilisation, while recognising that other international actors also had a part to play.
He said the challenge for Qatar and the EU now is to build on political dialogue and shared interests by turning them into sustained co-operation across security, energy, business, and diplomacy.
