articles.title: Greece Seeks More UAE Investment as Gateway to Europe - tovima.com
articles.summary: Greece Seeks More UAE Investment as Gateway to Europe  tovima.com
articles.full_text:
Μake us preferred on Google
Greece is seeking to attract more investment from the United Arab Emirates as the two countries deepen economic ties and explore opportunities across strategic sectors, including energy, technology, logistics and infrastructure.
On Thursday, Greece and the UAE announced 18 memoranda of understanding, agreements and commercial partnerships valued at €12.75 billion ($14.30 billion). Abu Dhabi also announced plans to invest an additional €15 billion in Greece, according to the Abu Dhabi Media Office and reported in Reuters.
The announcements were made at the UAE-Greece Strategic Forum in Athens, attended by Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis and Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan. The crown prince also held talks with Mitsotakis on expanding cooperation in energy, infrastructure and health care.
The additional investment plan builds on a joint investment initiative launched in 2022, under which the two countries committed €4 billion. The Abu Dhabi Media Office did not disclose the specific investments planned under the new initiative.
Speaking at Investopia in Athens on October 22, Greek Finance Minister Kyriakos Pierrakakis, who is also president of the Eurogroup, said closer ties with the UAE could help Greece serve as a gateway to the European Union’s single market, while the UAE could provide Greek businesses with access to the Middle East and other strategic economies. “We want to see more such investments coming,” Pierrakakis said, describing the two countries as natural partners.
He identified the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC), shipping, investment and logistics as areas with significant potential for cooperation. Realizing that potential, he said, would require governments to create favorable conditions and remove barriers, leaving businesses and investors to determine which companies and sectors could deliver the greatest opportunities.
The discussion took place during a session titled “Connecting Markets in a Time of Global Change,” which also featured UAE Minister of Investment Mohamed Hassan Alsuwaidi.
The UAE was Greece’s most important trading partner in 2024, with existing investments spanning energy, health care, technology and tourism.
Higher interest rates put pressure on Europe
Pierrakakis also warned that Europe was operating in a more demanding economic environment, despite demonstrating resilience.
He pointed to the rise in average European 10-year government bond yields, from 1.1% a decade ago to 4% currently, as evidence that the era of cheap capital had ended.
He identified six pressures contributing to the challenging environment: energy costs, geopolitical instability, greater fiscal constraints, increased investment needs, rising social spending and competition for capital from technology companies.
Europe faces growing investment demands, including spending on defense and measures to unlock its economic potential. Aging populations are also increasing pressure on public spending, he said, while the average European deficit is now twice what it was in the past.
Artificial intelligence is adding another dimension to the challenge. Pierrakakis described AI not only as a disruptive technology but also as a macroeconomic force, arguing that governments are competing with major technology companies that provide cloud-computing infrastructure to attract investment capital. That competition, he said, is pushing bond yields higher.
Given these pressures, he stressed the importance of collective action and identified the relationship with the UAE as a strategic priority for Greece.
AI requires faster policymaking
Pierrakakis said governments must move quickly to capitalize on artificial intelligence’s potential to improve productivity while managing its risks.
Technological change is now happening over weeks rather than years, he said, describing the pace of development as largely exponential. This creates a major challenge for policymakers, who must respond to emerging technologies while also addressing longstanding problems and implementing reforms that have been delayed for decades.
He also warned about the difficulty of preparing for unforeseen developments — what he called “unknown unknowns.”
Policymakers, he said, need the flexibility, speed, resilience and resources to manage both existing problems and unprecedented challenges.
UAE sees opportunities in logistics, energy and defense
Alsuwaidi said Greece’s geographic position could give it a greater role in trade between Europe and the Middle East, particularly amid disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, while commercial traffic continues through the Suez Canal.
Greece’s proximity to the canal could help it strengthen its position as a trading partner for countries in the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) and benefit from the redirection of trade flows, he said. Doing so would require greater investment in logistics, energy and essential infrastructure.
Alsuwaidi also highlighted opportunities for Greece and the UAE to work together on advanced technologies and defense solutions, including applications of artificial intelligence and robotics to protect borders and territory.
Greece’s large number of ports and the UAE’s wider regional security concerns offer potential grounds for cooperation, he said. He added that Greece could strengthen trade between Europe and the Middle East through the Red Sea and the Suez Canal.
AI, defense and health care top investment priorities
Asked where businesses from the two countries could work together, Alsuwaidi identified artificial intelligence, technology, defense, health care and modern logistics services as key areas.
He said the UAE could contribute its experience in AI and technology to joint projects, particularly in defense, health care and supply-chain services. Tourism also offers significant potential, he added, as Greece could attract more visitors amid changing international conditions.
However, Alsuwaidi said technology should remain the leading priority under current global circumstances, followed by defense and health care, which he described as sectors capable of changing people’s lives, with tourism also presenting an important opportunity.
The two officials’ remarks underscored a shared interest in expanding economic ties, using Greece’s position in southeastern Europe and the UAE’s investment and technological capabilities to develop new areas of cooperation.

articles.title: Carney, Recep Tayyip Erdogan launch strategic partnership to expand Canada-Turkey trade - The Jerusalem Post
articles.summary: Carney, Recep Tayyip Erdogan launch strategic partnership to expand Canada-Turkey trade  The Jerusalem Post
articles.full_text:
NATO allies Canada and Turkey upgraded their relations to a "strategic partnership" during the first bilateral visit by a Canadian prime minister on Thursday, as Mark Carney seeks new global trade partners to reduce reliance on the United States.
The agreement by Carney and Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan marks a significant thaw in diplomatic ties that had long been cool over Canadian concerns over human rights and a past embargo on sending weapons to Turkey.
The new partnership signed in Ankara focuses on trade and investment, defense and security, energy, and social and diplomatic ties. It aims to create jobs and opportunities for Canadian and Turkish companies to do more business together.
Carney is on a global trade blitz that he hopes will help buffer Canada from a trade war with the US, where President Donald Trump has applied sweeping tariffs and questioned the neighboring country's sovereignty.
Speaking next to Erdogan at Turkey's presidential palace, Carney said the strategic partnership would have four pillars and include a three-year action plan.
"We've planted the seeds of something new: a strategic partnership that will create new opportunities for our workers and businesses, and greater security and prosperity for both our peoples. With care and commitment, it will grow for generations to come," Carney said.
At the ceremony, Canadian and Turkish ministers signed cooperation deals on energy, defense and air transport.
'Long-standing disconnect'
Turkey, a major emerging market economy and regional military power, is seeking new investment and collaboration for its burgeoning defense industry, new nuclear power plants and mining sector.
Erdogan, who has led Turkey for 23 years, praised Carney as a leader with "common sense and acumen" on the world political stage.
"Today, we have alleviated the long-standing Turkey-Canada disconnect. Now, we are starting a new era between Turkey and Canada," Erdogan said. The two sides expect to raise their trade volume from $3 billion first to $5 billion and then to $10 billion, he said, without giving a timeframe.
Canadian and Turkish negotiators will kick off the first round of free trade talks next month in Ankara, Carney said, adding that Export Development Canada and Turkey's Eximbank would sign a new deal to boost companies' cooperation on projects in third nations.
Carney referenced the need to move forward with Turkey amid the "rupture" and "new world order," though neither he nor Erdogan mentioned the United States. Carney will meet prominent Turkish business leaders and investors in Istanbul on Friday.
In the energy sector, Canada and Turkey pledged to ramp up collaboration in areas such as nuclear energy, critical minerals, and liquefied natural gas.
Reuters first reported this week that the countries planned to sign a declaration deepening cooperation in the four areas outlined on Thursday.
Decreasing focus on rights
Although trade between Canada and Turkey is tiny, Turkey accounted for less than 0.3% of Canada’s total merchandise trade, or C$4.34 billion ($3.09 billion); bilateral trade has risen nearly 50% in the past five years.
Still, Canada sends nearly 70% of exports to the US.
"This trip is part of the geopolitical necessity of signaling to Americans that we are not sitting around waiting for them," said Bessma Momani, professor of political science at the University of Waterloo.
In the last year, Canada has signed more than 20 trade deals as part of Carney’s push to double non-US exports in the next decade. This included a trip to China to reset fractured relations, which was criticized because Canadian authorities previously said Beijing had interfered in at least two federal elections. China says it does not interfere in other countries' internal affairs.
Turkey's crackdown on the opposition since 2024 and new arrests targeting the LGBTQ+ community since September have drawn criticism from rights groups and some European officials. Ankara says the judiciary is independent, denying that investigations or court cases are politically motivated.
Carney has focused less on rights than his predecessors, analysts say.
"Carney will have to walk a very fine line in Turkey between opening new economic possibilities for Canada while trying to maintain Canada's middle power role in fighting for equality," said Anna Agathangelou, a professor of politics at York University.
Nuclear plant
At the NATO leaders' summit in July, Carney and Erdogan launched negotiations for a free-trade agreement, and Turkey also agreed to join Canada’s Defense, Security and Resilience Bank as a founding member.
Turkey has held talks with Canadian engineering firm AtkinsRealis as well as South Korea's Korea Electric Power Corporation and China's State Power Investment Corporation about potentially building its planned second and third nuclear power plants.
In 2024, Canada removed weapons-export controls on Turkey, including on optical technology used in drones that Turkey exports to dozens of nations. Canada mainly exports lentils, aircraft and electronics to Turkey, and imports medical devices, fishing vessels, aircraft engines and jewelry.

articles.title: UN, Israeli rights group warn of forced displacement in West Bank
articles.summary: The United Nations and an Israeli human rights group raised alarm Friday over escalating Israeli violence, sweeping closures and the threat of forced Palestinian displacement in th...
articles.full_text:
The United Nations and an Israeli human rights group raised alarm Friday over escalating Israeli violence, sweeping closures and the threat of forced Palestinian displacement in the occupied West Bank, as Israel ordered an immediate lockdown of Hebron following a deadly attack on its troops.
U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres expressed deep concern over deteriorating conditions across the occupied territory, where Israeli military operations, illegal settler attacks and restrictions on Palestinian movement have intensified.
"We are extremely alarmed by the intensifying violence that we're seeing in the occupied West Bank," U.N. spokesperson Stephane Dujarric told reporters Friday.
He said Guterres was particularly concerned about widespread Israeli-imposed closures affecting Palestinian communities, warning that the restrictions severely limited freedom of movement, access to essential services and livelihoods.
The U.N. chief also raised concerns over reports of home demolitions and the possible displacement of Palestinian residents in Hebron.
The warnings came as Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ordered the immediate closure of Hebron and instructed security forces to prepare for a full lockdown across the occupied West Bank following a deadly shooting incident.
The Israeli military said two soldiers were killed and three others seriously wounded in a gun battle in Hebron on Friday.
Separately, an Israeli human rights organization called for international pressure to prevent Israeli authorities from forcibly displacing Palestinians in response to the attack.
The organization urged action to stop measures that could uproot Palestinian communities as Israeli authorities considered further restrictions and security operations.
Dujarric said Guterres also condemned the violence resulting from record numbers of attacks by illegal Israeli settlers against Palestinians in 2026.
"He recalls Israel's obligation under international law as the occupying power to protect the Palestinian population from such attacks and to hold perpetrators to account," the spokesperson said.
The U.N. chief called for an immediate end to violence and urged all parties to avoid actions that could further destabilize the occupied territory.
"He calls on all parties to immediately cease all acts of violence, to exercise restraints, and refrain from action that could further inflame tensions," Dujarric said.
Violence across the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, has intensified since Israel launched its war on the Gaza Strip in October 2023.
Israeli military operations and attacks by illegal settlers have involved killings, arrests, home demolitions, the destruction of agricultural land and attacks on Palestinian property.
Palestinian communities have also faced restrictions on access to farmland, the burning of homes, mosques and vehicles, and displacement amid continued expansion of illegal Israeli settlements.
The latest closures have heightened concerns about the humanitarian consequences for Palestinian residents, particularly those already facing restrictions on movement and access to basic services.
Beyond the West Bank, Guterres expressed continued alarm over civilian casualties in the Gaza Strip, including the deaths of children, and severe restrictions on humanitarian assistance.
Dujarric said the U.N. chief was particularly concerned about obstacles to aid deliveries as winter approaches, warning of the growing risks facing vulnerable civilians.
He reiterated the urgent need to protect civilians and ensure humanitarian assistance reaches those in need.
The U.N.'s latest warnings underscore mounting international concern over the humanitarian situation in the occupied Palestinian territories, as Israeli military measures and settler violence continue to place Palestinian communities under increasing pressure.

articles.title: Israeli strikes kill at least 4 Palestinians in Gaza despite cease-fire
articles.summary: Israeli strikes and gunfire killed at least four Palestinians across the Gaza Strip on Thursday, as continued attacks underscored the fragility of a U.S.-brokered ceasefire that ha...
articles.full_text:
Israeli strikes and gunfire killed at least four Palestinians across the Gaza Strip on Thursday, as continued attacks underscored the fragility of a U.S.-brokered ceasefire that has failed to halt the violence or pave the way for reconstruction, health officials said.
In Gaza City, an Israeli strike hit a vehicle in the Tel al-Hawa neighborhood, killing at least one person, according to medics.
Earlier reports put the death toll at two. Images from the scene showed crowds gathering around the burning wreckage as emergency crews in orange vests sprayed the vehicle with water.
Gaza’s Hamas-led Interior Ministry said the strike killed a noncommissioned officer from the drug-control police department and wounded another officer. The two were returning from an assignment when their vehicle was hit, according to the ministry.
Elsewhere, strikes killed a Palestinian man riding a bicycle in the southern city of Khan Younis and another man near the Nuseirat refugee camp in central Gaza, medics said. Gunfire killed a woman near the Jabalia refugee camp in the north.
Israel’s military claimed it had struck Hamas members in Khan Younis, Nuseirat and Gaza City. It said it was unaware of the reported shooting in Jabalia.
The latest deaths come amid renewed Israeli attacks on targets it identifies as Hamas positions.
Israel accuses the Palestinian group of rebuilding its arsenal and carrying out attacks in violation of the cease-fire. Hamas denies the allegations and accuses Israel of undermining the agreement through continued military operations.
The cease-fire, brokered by the United States and implemented in October 2025, envisioned an eventual end to the Gaza genocide, the withdrawal of Israeli forces and the reconstruction of the devastated territory.
However, negotiations have made little progress on key issues, particularly Hamas’ disarmament and the extent of an Israeli military withdrawal.
Israeli airstrikes, gunfire and other military operations have continued despite the truce, leaving Palestinians exposed to further casualties and delaying efforts to rebuild homes and essential infrastructure.
Gaza health officials say at least 1,500 Palestinians have been killed since the cease-fire began. Israel, meanwhile, says four of its soldiers have been killed in Gaza over the same period.
The continued violence has deepened concerns about the agreement’s ability to deliver lasting security or meaningful relief to the territory’s population, much of which has been displaced by more than two years of war.
Palestinian authorities say more than 74,000 people have been killed in Israel’s military campaign in Gaza, which began following Hamas' incursion into southern Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, killing about 1,200 people, according to Israeli figures.
The Gaza Health Ministry has also reported more than 175,000 injuries. The figures are widely cited by the United Nations and international organizations, although the full toll remains uncertain, with victims believed to remain buried beneath destroyed buildings.

articles.title: US strikes on Iran now serve the blockade - Iran International
articles.summary: US strikes on Iran now serve the blockade  Iran International
articles.full_text:
A possible resumption of US strikes on Iran would serve an increasingly economic war, weakening Tehran’s ability to challenge a blockade that Washington appears prepared to maintain for the foreseeable future.
A strike on Iran could "absolutely" come this weekend, the US ambassador to Turkey, Tom Barrack, said Friday, and the administration hasn’t said what it would be for.
The New York Times reports that US and Israeli planners have drawn up a short, intensive campaign for after the November 3 midterms, aimed at Iran’s missile and drone arsenal, nuclear sites and energy infrastructure.
Critics read the reports as proof that there is no strategy anymore. That reads the war through the lens of February, when the economic campaign existed to support the war. Whether the administration designed it this way or simply ended up here, the strikes now serve the economic campaign, which is proving more harmful to the regime than the strikes ever were.
Washington has committed to the blockade and treats the strikes as optional. Speaking to reporters Friday, President Trump said the choice was whether to finish it off or let it wither, and that with oil moving through Hormuz the US was getting everything it wanted. Mike Waltz, the US ambassador to the United Nations, told the Financial Times the same day that the president and the Navy can maintain the blockade for the foreseeable future while the administration keeps tightening economic pressure.
The US is now running a siege. It has sharply restricted Iran’s access to oil buyers, international finance and regional trade. The job of the military is to keep the cordon from being broken. The shift in strategy came in July, when the US restored the blockade after the June memorandum collapsed and the strikes that followed were about the strait.
Central Command said its July strikes were meant to degrade Iran’s ability to attack commercial shipping. The next round of strikes would be the first planned campaign since the blockade and the sanctions began doing real damage to the regime.
Iran’s imports since the war began show its priority — bringing in the supplies it needs to be able to fight its way out of the blockade. It is bringing in truck parts, missile fuel ingredients and missile and drone components to rebuild the launchers and stockpiles. The Wall Street Journal counted about 1,300 shipments of dual-use components from Chinese suppliers to Iran’s defense ministry in the first half of the year.
On October 1 the Treasury sanctioned Iran’s truck and auto makers, which it called an essential part of Iran’s defense industrial base, and the suppliers in Turkey, the Emirates and East Asia feeding them parts. Iran is assembling missiles from stockpiled components in small numbers, the Journal reported in September, and the blockade has made the solid-fuel components it can’t make harder to import.
Iran loaded no crude oil onto tankers in September, according to Bloomberg. CENTCOM says the blockade has stopped $25 billion in oil exports. The United Arab Emirates halted all trade and financial dealings with Iran in August. The regime has no way to persuade its own base or the Persian Gulf states that it has an answer.
That leaves Tehran a short list of cards to play against the blockade and the sanctions.
The first is attacking commercial shipping in the strait. Maritime security sources recorded at least 12 attacks on tankers around the Strait of Hormuz in the week to October 5, the highest weekly total of the war.
The second is pressuring its neighbors. Iran threatens Persian Gulf energy infrastructure, US bases and undersea cables, and it has the Houthis at Bab el-Mandeb, all meant to push the Persian Gulf states to lobby Washington to end the blockade.
The third is to strain US munition supplies. Mohsen Rezaei, Iran’s security chief, said this week that a long war favors Iran because the test is which side can sustain a cycle of production, deployment and response.
The fourth is to keep offering a deal that it likely won’t make. Tehran’s standing offer is to reopen the strait in seven days in exchange for ending the blockade, easing oil sanctions and releasing frozen assets.
The fifth is the nuclear program, which the regime can negotiate to death over enrichment and dangle in front of Washington for the same price.
A strike goes down that list. The missile and drone arsenal the Times describes, and the launchers, mine-layers, naval sites, radars and air defenses CENTCOM has hit since July, are the hardware behind the regime’s threat to the strait and its neighbors.
Fewer launchers means fewer ships hit and a weaker threat to the Persian Gulf. Hitting stockpiles and production sites limits its ability to strain and outlast US munition supplies, and a strike tests Rezaei’s claim directly. Destroying enough of those capabilities would weaken Iran’s offer to stop attacking shipping in exchange for lifting the blockade.
Washington would have less reason to pay for a threat Iran could no longer credibly sustain. Hitting Pickaxe Mountain doesn’t end the nuclear program, but it leaves Tehran less to bargain with when it asks for sanctions relief.
Holding a blockade is expensive. Destroyers are doing work that cheap systems should do, and the Navy is stretched thin. Fewer Iranian launchers firing at the escort mission means the Navy can hold the line longer without forcing a decision in Washington.
The regime has shown it will take the strikes. Ali Khamenei and Ali Larijani are dead, Mojtaba Khamenei succeeded his father, and Tehran still won’t concede on any deal the US could accept. What it can’t take is the economic war.
The blockade turned the clock against Tehran. The regime’s strategy since February has been to wait — for the administration to lose patience, for the midterms, for the next policy swing.
The US can hold a blockade for the foreseeable future at a cost it can carry. A prolonged loss of oil revenue will make Tehran’s strategy of waiting out Washington increasingly difficult to sustain. The strikes exist to keep that clock running.

articles.title: Attack in the West Bank kills 2 Israeli soldiers, and other Mideast news - AP News
articles.summary: Attack in the West Bank kills 2 Israeli soldiers, and other Mideast news  AP NewsIsrael begins demolitions in West Bank city after two soldiers killed in shooting attack  CNNPalestinian Gunmen Open Fire on Israelis in the West Bank, Officials Say  The New York TimesNetanyahu Calls for West Bank Lockdown After Deadly Attack  WSJIsrael launches collective punishment campaign in Hebron after two soldiers killed  The Guardian
articles.full_text:
Israel said it prevented a “terror attack” on Israeli civilians Friday when the military killed two gunmen who had fatally shot two Israeli soldiers. The shooting came days before Tuesday’s election, when Israeli voters will decide whether to give Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu another term.
In Jordan, gunmen opened fire inside a church, killing seven people and wounding 40.
Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Friday. Read our full coverage here.
AP correspondent Charles de Ledesma reports Israeli settlers have attacked West Bank villages, injuring Palestinian and a foreign journalist during the olive harvest.
Israel conducts searches in Hebron area where gunmen had operated
Israel’s military said that, in response to the killing of two soldiers and wounding of others in the West Bank earlier that day, its forces had begun “conducting precise, targeted and thorough searches” in the area of Hebron from which the two gunmen had operated.
It added in a statement late Friday that this operation was expected to continue for several days, and all residents living in the area will only be able to leave through three designated exit points following “questioning and security screening.”
The army said it has started demolishing infrastructure that poses a “threat” and that its soldiers continue operating across the West Bank.
Earlier Friday, Israel’s prime minister’s office said it had ordered the army to prepare for a full closure of the West Bank. The prime minister’s office said it had instructed the army to close off the occupied West Bank, where the shooting occurred.
Israel’s army says it killed 2 gunmen who killed soldiers
Israel’s military said its soldiers shot and killed two men who had launched an attack near the city of Hebron in the occupied West Bank on Friday morning. Two soldiers were killed and three others lightly wounded in the attack.
The army said it prevented a “terror attack against Israeli civilians” and that the gunmen had an M16 rifle and a handgun.
Following the attack, Israel’s prime minister’s office said it had ordered the army to prepare for a full closure of the West Bank.
The prime minister’s office said it had instructed the army to close off the occupied West Bank, where the shooting occurred.
US to reduce staffing at four Mideast embassies as fears of Houthi attacks rise
The State Department is reducing staff at four U.S. embassies in the Middle East after receiving intelligence that Iran has stepped up efforts to target American personnel in the region and elsewhere.
In a memo sent Friday to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said his teams “have received intelligence that Iran has substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel.”
“The lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against U.S. citizens have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries,” Clayton wrote.
The memo was obtained by The Associated Press and reported earlier by Axios. Three U.S. officials, speaking on condition of anonymity due to the sensitivity of the matter, confirmed that the memo was sent to Rubio in his capacity as secretary of state and national security adviser.
The memo emerged shortly after the State Department announced it is reducing staff at the U.S. embassies in Jordan, Lebanon, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates. The three officials said the threats from Iran and Yemen’s Iranian-backed Houthi rebels are related to the staffing changes.
— By Matthew Lee
Churchgoers in Jordan attacked during funeral
In Jordan, gunmen opened fire during a funeral at a church Friday, killing seven people and wounding 40 others, authorities said.
The shooting took place at a Greek Orthodox church in Karak, home to a minority Christian population, about 180 kilometers (110 miles) south of the capital Amman.
Jordan’s Health Minister Ibrahim al-Budour said that two of those wounded are in critical condition.
Images being broadcast on Jordanian state television show two gunmen who appear to be holding pistols approaching the church and firing shots. A third man who appears to be holding a semiautomatic rifle then approaches and opens fire, and all three then run toward the church.
A government statement said that the attack was “carried out by unknown assailants,” but didn’t say whether any gunmen were captured or killed. It said that “investigations are underway at full speed.”
In 2016, Islamic State militants launched an attack on the Karak Castle, a popular tourist site, killing 14 people, including a Canadian tourist. No group immediately claimed responsibility for Friday’s attack.
Arab parties ask Israel’s top court to bar armed poll observers
Arab political parties running in Israel’s national election have asked the Supreme Court to ban partisan election observers from carrying guns at polling stations.
The petition, filed Thursday with the Israel-based legal group Adalah, said the ban was essential to protecting public safety and ensuring a free and fair election on Tuesday.
It followed announcements by Jewish parties led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich that they planned to send about 2,000 election observers to Arab neighborhoods, citing allegations of voter fraud.
Palestinians make up about 20% of Israel’s population. Arab-led parties could prove decisive in the upcoming election, the first since Hamas’ Oct. 7, 2023, attack, if Jewish parties are willing to join them in a governing coalition.
Israeli strikes in Gaza kill 3
Strikes by Israel’s army killed three people on Friday in southern Gaza and Gaza City, according to local health officials.
The first strike in southern Gaza killed one person. Israel’s military said it targeted a Hamas militant.
The second strike killed two people in Gaza City, but Israel’s military did not immediately comment on the strike.
Grieving relatives of the two people killed in Gaza City gathered in the courtyard of the Shifa hospital, where the casualties were taken.
More than 1,500 Palestinians in Gaza have been killed by the Israeli military since the ceasefire between Israel and Hamas began in October 2025, according to the territory’s health ministry. The ministry maintains detailed records and is regarded as generally reliable by U.N. agencies and independent experts. Part of the Hamas-run government, the ministry does not distinguish between civilians and militants but says women and children make up nearly half of those killed.

articles.title: Iran has detailed plans to hit Gulf undersea cables if war resumes, officials say - Aaj English TV
articles.summary: Iran has detailed plans to hit Gulf undersea cables if war resumes, officials say  Aaj English TV
articles.full_text:
4 min read
Tehran has drawn up detailed plans to target undersea communications cables in the Gulf if the United States and Israel attack Iran again, two senior Iranian security officials told Reuters.
Their comments followed warnings by Iranian officials that undersea cables in the region could become targets in any renewed conflict if diplomacy with Washington collapses.
The two Iranian security officials, speaking on condition of anonymity, gave few details and did not say how or where exactly Tehran would carry out such attacks. But one of them said Iran would aim to prevent repairs after any attacks to prolong disruptions to communications, including internet connections.
“If Iran is attacked, there will be no more red lines … from undersea cables to military bases, including covert ones,” one of the officials said.
The official warned Washington not to “play with fire”, and said Iran had full access to the undersea cables and could easily destroy them.
Yadollah Javani, the deputy head of political affairs for Iran’s Revolutionary Guards (IRGC), said on Wednesday that Iran could target seven major internet cables beneath the Strait of Hormuz if Iranian infrastructure came under attack.
Undersea cables carry around 99% of global internet traffic, according to the International Telecommunication Union, a UN agency. But the global impact of such attacks by Iran could be limited, as less than 1% of international bandwidth passes through the Strait of Hormuz, said Alan Mauldin, research director at telecommunications research firm TeleGeography.
The strait separates Iran and Oman, linking the Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea.
The US Department of State and Iran’s Foreign Ministry did not respond to Reuters’ requests for comment on the Iranian security officials’ remarks. There was no immediate comment from Gulf states.
‘STRONGER RESPONSE’
The plans for possible attacks on undersea cables reflect a conviction in Iran’s leadership that a renewed US military campaign would have to be met with a stronger response than before.
Top security official Mohsen Rezaei warned this month that US-linked digital infrastructure across the Gulf, including data centres and AI facilities, could be targeted in a renewed conflict.
Washington’s Gulf allies have invested heavily in such infrastructure and they “should hold Washington, not Tehran, responsible for any damage to undersea cables,” the second Iranian security official said.
Alex Vatanka, director of the Iran programme at the Middle East Institute in Washington, said such threats were intended to deter renewed conflict and put pressure on Washington by making Gulf governments and US companies fear for their investments in the region.
“Tehran wants Gulf states and corporate executives to press (US President Donald) Trump over the risks his policies pose to their investment plans,” said Vatanka.
Multiple cable cuts could slow internet services and disrupt financial transactions, e-commerce and cloud computing, analysts said. The impact would depend on how operators rerouted traffic and the capacity available on alternative connections, Mauldin said.
Restoring connections during wartime could be difficult, experts said, and higher insurance costs and delays in obtaining permits to enter territorial waters could further complicate repairs.
The Red Sea could offer a more significant target than the Strait of Hormuz, particularly if Iran had support from its Houthi allies in Yemen, though Tehran has made no public statement indicating it plans to target cables there.
The Red Sea carries data between Europe, East Africa and Asia, with capacity routed through it accounting for about 3% of global international demand and around 10% of traffic travelling between regions, Mauldin said.
Gulf governments have been investing heavily in technology to diversify beyond oil and become global artificial intelligence hubs, deepening ties with US technology firms.
Iranian strikes directly hit two Amazon Web Services facilities in the UAE in March and damaged infrastructure near one of its facilities in Bahrain. The IRGC named US tech companies including Microsoft, Google, Apple and Nvidia as legitimate targets at the height of the war in March.
Land-based connections can provide alternative routes for internet traffic, and Gulf states and US technology companies are investing in additional infrastructure to improve resilience.
Microsoft plans to invest more than $400 million in subsea and terrestrial connectivity across the Middle East by 2030.

articles.title: Makkah pact ratification completed by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia: FO - The Express Tribune
articles.summary: Makkah pact ratification completed by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia: FO  The Express Tribune
articles.full_text:
Spokesperson says agreement has 16 articles, no hidden provisions; endorses text presented in the Turkish parliament
The Foreign Office confirmed on Friday that Pakistan and Saudi Arabia have completed their ratification processes for the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement (MJDA), while Türkiye is undertaking the requisite legal procedures for the agreement’s ratification.
“Each country follows its own constitutional and legal procedures for the approval and ratification of international agreements,” Foreign Office Spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan said during the question and answer session after the weekly press briefing held in Islamabad.
The spokesperson said Pakistan and the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia had completed their ratification processes, while Türkiye was pursuing the requisite procedures in accordance with its legal framework.
Asked whether the agreement contained any undisclosed clauses, particularly in view of Pakistan’s separate defence agreement with Saudi Arabia, the spokesperson said the MJDA comprised 16 articles and contained no hidden provisions.
🔊 Transcript of the Weekly Press Briefing by the Spokesperson https://t.co/IBRZCZjJ2R
🔗⬇️ pic.twitter.com/APzZlHao5i
— Ministry of Foreign Affairs - Pakistan (@ForeignOfficePk) October 23, 2026
“There are no hidden provisions; the agreement is explicit and clear in its provisions and articles,” Khan stressed, adding that Pakistan endorsed the text released by the Turkish parliament in the media.
He further outlined that matters related to the agreement’s ratification and operationalisation are deliberated through the trilateral Strategic Political and Defence Committee, whose latest meeting was held on October 5.
Emphasising the defensive nature of the MJDA, Khan said it was consistent with the United Nations Charter and aimed at promoting regional peace, security and stability.
In response to a question about an International Crisis Group report warning of the risk of renewed conflict between Pakistan and India amid increased militant activity in Indian-occupied Jammu and Kashmir, the spokesperson said Islamabad wanted all disputes to be resolved peacefully and in accordance with international law.
“From Pakistan’s perspective, war is not a solution to any issue,” the spokesperson said, adding that disputes over Jammu and Kashmir and the Indus Waters Treaty should be addressed through dialogue and adherence to international law.
While acknowledging that the issues posed a potential risk of conflict, Khan dispelled chances of another military confrontation with India and reiterated that Pakistan was fully prepared to protect its sovereignty and territorial integrity.
On the possibility of another false-flag operation by India, the spokesperson said it could not be ruled out.
“We are prepared for all eventualities,” Khan cautioned.
US ties and Indus Waters Treaty

articles.title: DIFC Innovation Hub establishes Geospatial Accelerator advances Dubai's ambition to lead converging space, AI economy - Big News Network.com
articles.summary: DIFC Innovation Hub establishes Geospatial Accelerator advances Dubai's ambition to lead converging space, AI economy  Big News Network.com
articles.full_text:
DUBAI, 23rd October, 2026 (WAM) -- DIFC Innovation Hub and the Mohammed Bin Rashid Space Centre (MBRSC), today announced significant progress in the Geospatial Accelerator, the inaugural programme under the Space for Earth Labs platform, marked by the selection of several international scale-ups.
The platform has been established by DIFC Innovation Hub in partnership with the Mohammed Bin Rashid Space Centre (MBRSC) and Relm Insurance to connect space and Earth Observation (EO) technologies with artificial intelligence, commercial expertise and industry demand. It will strengthen the space sector's contribution to the national economy and supports the objectives of the National Space Strategy 2030, positioning Dubai at the forefront of the converging space and AI economy.
Based at the DIFC Innovation Hub, Space for Earth Labs provides a single point of entry for companies seeking to apply space-derived data to commercial and public-sector challenges. The Geospatial Accelerator, was launched at the Dubai Airshow in November 2025. The programme attracted 73 applications from 24 countries of which 63 were assessed as valid and 45 progressed to interview.
This led to the selection of ten scale-ups including AtlasAI, FlyPix AI, Geospatial Insight, GHGSat, Latitudo40, Little Place Labs, SatSure, SparkGeo, Stellaria and V-Nova. These firms will now be matched to three UAE public sector organisations: FADA (part of EDGE Group), Ministry of Energy & Infrastructure - National Maritime Centre (NMC) and The Dubai Civil Defence General Command, along with two private sector organisations: Buro Happold (a professional services firm), and Liva Insurance, part of Liva Group. Together, they will develop proof-of-concept pilots (PoCs) across maritime and infrastructure, insurance and risk, the built environment, public safety, and geospatial intelligence.
Each use case pairs a scaleup with a real operational challenge faced by a UAE entity, translating space and AI innovation into applied solutions across maritime safety, insurance, the built environment, and public safety.
Through the Geospatial Accelerator and Space for Earth Labs, Dubai is building the marketplace that connects frontier space and AI technologies with institutional customers and serious investors. At present, Earth Observation (EO) contributes an estimated USD 440bn to global GDP while the broader AI-in-geospatial market is forecast to grow at 19.5 per cent annually through 2028. Major technology companies have also dedicated capital to AI-enabled environmental applications, including AWS, Google, Microsoft and Nvidia.
Mohammad Alblooshi, Chief Executive Officer at the DIFC Innovation Hub, said: "The Geospatial Accelerator demonstrates how Dubai can turn frontier technology into economic opportunity by bringing together space, artificial intelligence, finance and industry around real-world challenges. DIFC established this initiative because our role extends beyond financial services: we are building the platforms, partnerships and investment ecosystem that enable emerging technologies to move from innovation and proof-of-concept to commercial scale, whilst supporting the innovation objectives of the Dubai Economic Agenda (D33)."
Saeed AlMansoori, Director of the Remote Sensing Department, MBRSC, said: "Through the Geospatial Accelerator, MBRSC is helping create a direct pathway to translate Earth Observation data into actionable insights that address real operational priorities across the UAE. By working closely with government and industry partners, we are expanding the practical use of space-derived data across sectors, demonstrating its wider value and supporting the objectives of the UAE National Space Strategy 2030."
Joseph Ziolkowski, CEO and Founder, Relm Insurance, said: "The value of this programme is that it connects space and AI companies to real operational problems, where innovation ultimately has to earn the trust of the institutions adopting it. Insurance can be a powerful enabler of that trust. As these technologies move from proof of concept into real-world deployment, they need an insurance partner willing to understand the technology, the use case, and the evolving risks, while also being flexible enough to build coverage around them. Relm's role is to provide that support, giving innovators and their customers greater confidence to test, adopt, and ultimately scale solutions that can have meaningful real-world impact."
As a real outcome-driven platform dedicated to SpaceTech scale-ups, the initiative advances the Dubai Economic Agenda (D33) which aims to double the size of Dubai's economy over the next decade and consolidate its position among the top three global cities.
Selected scale-ups will present their proof-of-concept solutions at the Dubai AI Festival in October 2026 further amplifying the programme's innovations to a global audience including top venture capitalists, enterprises, government agencies and ministries.

HUMAIN and DataVolt have signed a preliminary agreement with Nebius to supply up to 50MW of data-center capacity at NEOM's Oxagon site, making Nebius the anchor customer for the planned 360MW AI campus.
HUMAIN, a PIF-owned artificial intelligence company, and DataVolt, a developer, owner and operator of digital infrastructure, have announced a preliminary framework agreement with Nebius, an AI cloud company, for data centre capacity at Oxagon, NEOM's industrial city on Saudi Arabia's Red Sea coast.
Under the proposed framework, Nebius would become an anchor customer for the planned AI campus, with the contemplated offtake representing up to 50MW — half of the initial 100MW currently under construction as part of the first phase's planned 360MW. The framework outlines a proposed international customer allocation six weeks after construction began. The proposed capacity allocation is expected to become operational in phases from Q4 2027.
The agreement involves HUMAIN's AI infrastructure plans, DataVolt's infrastructure development work, and Nebius's demand for data-centre capacity to serve its customer base. The campus is intended to support AI workloads, with Nebius expected to deploy NVIDIA computing infrastructure under the agreement.
The companies say the arrangement combines NVIDIA computing infrastructure with energy and time-to-market factors available at NEOM's Oxagon site.
DataVolt said reaching an advanced stage of commercial engagement with Nebius within six weeks of starting construction reflects its ability to accelerate project delivery and secure commercial commitments. CEO Rajit Nanda said competitive infrastructure costs and rapid deployment are important in the AI computing market, and said the company aims to combine Saudi Arabia's energy resources with its execution approach to position the Kingdom as an exporter of digital capacity.
NEOM said the agreement between HUMAIN, DataVolt and Nebius reflects international demand for AI-related infrastructure. Managing director and CEO Eng. Aiman Al-Mudaifer said Oxagon is being developed as an integrated site intended to help technology companies expand capacity and support related industries.
The agreement was signed during NVIDIA's GTC Berlin conference.
HUMAIN said the agreement supports its plans to build infrastructure, computing platforms, AI models and applications. DataVolt said it reinforces its approach to developing digital infrastructure aligned with customer demand. For Nebius, the agreement represents an expansion of infrastructure capacity to support its AI cloud business.

articles.title: Yemen, Bab al-Mandab and Saudi Arabia: Tehran’s strategic calculus in the balance - Middle East Eye
articles.summary: Yemen, Bab al-Mandab and Saudi Arabia: Tehran’s strategic calculus in the balance  Middle East Eye
articles.full_text:
Recent Houthi attacks on Saudi oil infrastructure and the Yemeni group’s growing leverage over Red Sea shipping have played to Iran's strategic advantage, increasing pressure on Riyadh and strengthening Tehran’s position in the regional conflict.
The Houthis’ capture in September of the strategic Yemeni port city of Mokha from Saudi-backed government forces has placed a vital alternative route for Saudi oil exports through the Bab al-Mandab Strait at risk.
For Tehran, this presents an opportunity to drive up oil prices and pressure US President Donald Trump to end the war, while linking threats to shipping through Bab al-Mandab to disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz.
But as Saudi Arabia sought Tehran’s help in containing the Houthis, Iran must also contend with the limits of its influence over the Houthis, who have their own domestic objectives.
The escalation has also left Iran facing a delicate balancing act of supporting a key regional ally without allowing the conflict to spiral beyond its control.
'Not an Iranian proxy'
Tensions between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, officially called Ansar Allah, have been simmering for months.
In July, Tehran reportedly sent a plane carrying between 10 and 21 the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) personnel, including senior commanders, to Yemen, according to sources speaking to Reuters, to challenge the Saudi-led blockade.
A senior conservative source told Middle East Eye that the Saudi ambassador to Iran, who has a security background, subsequently met Iranian officials in an effort to defuse tensions.
The source said that "Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi had signalled his readiness to travel to Saudi Arabia at Riyadh’s request, but the trip did not take place".
According to the source, Riyadh wanted Tehran to pressure the Houthis to halt their attacks and threats. Tehran, in turn, called for the Saudi blockade to be lifted and offered to mediate between the warring sides.
The source added that Pakistani officials had also repeatedly travelled to Tehran or contacted Araghchi by phone, urging Iran to use its influence to persuade the Houthis to de-escalate.
However, a senior source close to the establishment told MEE that Saudi Arabia and Pakistan were mistaken in viewing the Houthis as an Iranian proxy.
While Hezbollah in Lebanon could be considered an extension of Iran, the source argued, the Houthis have acted according to their own interests.
If the Houthis were simply an Iranian proxy, he said, they would have blocked all ships from passing through the Bab al-Mandab Strait, including American vessels, rather than targeting only Saudi-linked shipping.
"Saudi asked Iran to help secure a ceasefire for several weeks, however, Houthies didn't agree," the source added.
On 11 October, following two Houthi attacks on Riyadh's main airport that killed 13 people, Araghchi said in a phone call with his Saudi counterpart that Tehran was ready to help initiate talks between Saudi Arabia and Ansar Allah and work toward a political solution to the crisis in Yemen.
An unresolved conflict
A Saudi affairs analyst writing for a reformist media outlet in Iran argued that the 2022 ceasefire between the Houthis and Riyadh, which largely halted fighting in Yemen, had not resolved the crisis but merely pushed it to the margins.
The crisis, he told MEE, had resurfaced at the slightest sign of regional escalation because its underlying causes remained unresolved, while security around the Bab al-Mandab Strait had become increasingly intertwined with developments in the Strait of Hormuz.
As a result, he added, Yemen’s crisis was evolving from an internal conflict, and later one largely confined to the Arabian Peninsula, into a broader regional and international confrontation.
The analyst argued that in addition to immediate security concerns, Riyadh’s insistence on a military approach also stemmed from its view of Yemen as a matter of national and regional prestige and historical credibility.
In the analyst’s view, this mindset, coupled with Riyadh’s perception of its eminent role in the Arabian Peninsula, has left Saudi Arabia unwilling to adopt a more flexible approach to Yemen, recognise the Houthis or accept the emergence of a Shia-led government on its border.
Sanaa’s new rules of engagement
Following the Houthis’ rapid advances along the Red Sea coast and around the Bab al-Mandab Strait, Riyadh turned to Beijing last month for help, as the group’s gains threatened Saudi oil exports and shipping.
Iranian sources told Reuters that China had privately urged Tehran to rein in the Houthis to prevent further escalation along vital energy routes on which China depends.
A conservative analyst close to Iran's power centres told MEE that strikes on vital installations deep inside Saudi territory signalled that Sanaa’s response to Saudi Arabia’s actions and blockade against Yemen was moving beyond conventional military retaliation.
In recent weeks, the Houthis have attacked Saudi airports several times, including King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and Abha International Aiport in Asir province.
On 10 October, an attack on King Khalid airport killed at least 12 people and wounded more than 300. The following day, another attack on the airport killed one person and wounded nearly a dozen others.
The Houthis, the analyst said, were seeking to establish a new set of battlefield equations: “Riyadh for Sanaa”, “airport for airport”, “oil for oil” and “blockade for blockade”.
“The phrase ‘Riyadh for Sanaa’ is more than a political slogan,” the analyst added.
“It reflects an attempt to redefine the relationship between attack and retaliation, signalling that, according to Sanaa’s leadership, Yemen’s territory will no longer be the only battleground.”
The analyst said the military message was inseparable from the political one: Sanaa wanted to demonstrate that continuing the war would carry consequences for Saudi Arabia itself.
Tehran faces a big danger
A Iranian reformist academic said Iran risks losing its strategic position as regional and international actors move towards a new security arrangement around the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden. He believes Tehran must therefore seek to ease tensions between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis.
In July, Saudi Arabia and 13 other countries announced the creation of a maritime military coalition to safeguard freedom of navigation through the three waterways. The significance of the alignment, the academic argued, extends well beyond the immediate confrontation with Ansar Allah.
'The phrase ‘Riyadh for Sanaa’ is more than a political slogan. It reflects an attempt to redefine the relationship between attack and retaliation'
- Conservative analyst
He noted that what initially appeared to be a campaign focused on countering Houthi attacks on commercial shipping may be evolving into a broader effort to establish a lasting regional maritime security framework, with the Bab el-Mandab Strait at its centre.
Countries with different strategic priorities – and, in some cases, competing interests – are increasingly finding common ground around the security of vital maritime routes.
This, he added, could have far-reaching implications for global trade and the regional balance of power.
"For Tehran, the implications are particularly serious. The challenge is no longer confined to its relationship with the Houthis or its ability to influence events in Yemen,” he said.
“It concerns the possibility that a new regional arrangement could gradually constrain Iran’s strategic reach and diminish its influence over one of the world’s most important maritime corridors."
The academic’s central concern is that Tehran may be focusing too heavily on immediate tactical calculations while overlooking a much larger transformation unfolding around it.
Linked outcomes
Iran’s Tasnim News Agency, an outlet affiliated with the IRGC, has argued that the outcome of the US-Iran war and the future of the Strait of Hormuz will directly affect the conflict in Yemen, particularly the strategic balance around the Bab al-Mandab Strait and Saudi oil exports through the Red Sea.
Houthi restrictions on Red Sea shipping, combined with disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, have increased pressure on Saudi Arabia’s energy exports.
'The challenge for Iran is a new regional arrangement could gradually constrain its strategic reach...over one of the world’s most important maritime corridors'
- Reformist academic
“Whatever outcome emerges in the Strait of Hormuz will have a direct impact on the Yemen file, whether positive or negative,” Tasnim wrote, quoting an Iranian expert who warned that weakening the Houthis or ending their control over parts of the Red Sea coastline could have serious consequences for Iran.
“If the Houthis are weakened, lose access to the Red Sea and its coastline, or if the United States, the West and Saudi Arabia secure guarantees that Saudi energy infrastructure is no longer threatened from the south, the consequences for Iran could be highly damaging, giving Washington and its allies greater freedom to act against Tehran,” the outlet quoted the expert as saying.
Tasnim urged Tehran to step up its diplomatic support for the Houthis, arguing that Iran should not expect its allies to defend it if it fails to support them.
"When we do not deploy all our capabilities to defend an ally, we should not expect that ally to deploy all of its capabilities to defend us," the expert said.

articles.title: How Saudi Arabia Overextended Itself - Compact Mag
articles.summary: How Saudi Arabia Overextended Itself  Compact Mag
articles.full_text:
There are few projects that better capture Mohammed bin Salman’s ambitions for Saudi Arabia than NEOM. Announced in 2017 and launched as part of Vision 2030, the vast development on the Red Sea was supposed to demonstrate what the kingdom could accomplish when combining its almost limitless capital with cutting-edge technology and political will. In its promotional materials, the centerpiece of the project, The Line, was presented as an entirely new kind of city stretching 170 kilometers through the desert. Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund described NEOM as a “living laboratory” in which “innovation will chart the course for a new future.” Speaking in 2022, MBS declared the project nothing short of a “civilizational revolution” that would “challenge the traditional flat, horizontal cities” and “shine a light on alternative ways to live.”
But in recent years, skyrocketing costs, changing economic and political circumstances, and the monumental engineering, infrastructure, and logistical demands of the project have forced the Saudi government to scale back its ambitions. By 2024, construction plans were reportedly concentrated on an initial 2.4-kilometer section of the proposed 170-kilometer city. By October 2026, the Public Investment Fund acknowledged that The Line was no longer a priority for completion by 2030, and plans for a spectacular elevated World Cup stadium were reportedly shelved. It seems unlikely that whatever emerges from the deserts of Tabuk Province will be anything like what the marketing videos and slide decks once promised.
NEOM, in both its conception and its fate, is a Babelian monument to the belief that sufficient wealth and political will could overcome the constraints of geography, labor, and technology. As such, the scheme is emblematic of a deeper contradiction within MBS’s political project. Rising to power in the mid-2010s, Saudi Arabia’s de facto ruler sought to use the accumulated rents of the old oil economy to construct a new social order—a technocratic, hypermodern, consumption-oriented society capable of projecting economic and political power far beyond the Arabian Peninsula. This enterprise brought significant changes to everyday life, including curbs on the religious police, greater freedom for women to drive and travel independently, the reopening of cinemas, and the expansion of public entertainment.

articles.title: How have the wars in the Middle East changed oil transport flows? - Balkanweb.com
articles.summary: How have the wars in the Middle East changed oil transport flows?  Balkanweb.com
articles.full_text:
The escalation of the war in the Middle East is changing global oil transport flows, putting pressure on two of the world's most important maritime corridors, the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb.
Attacks, missile and drone threats, and the risk of naval mines have restricted navigation and increased the costs of transporting energy.
According to data from the company Windward, at the end of September an average of 31 ships passed through the Strait of Hormuz per day, down from 138 per day before the start of the war with Iran.
The decline in maritime traffic has also been accompanied by a significant decrease in oil transport. Before the conflict, about 20 million barrels of oil passed through the strait per day, while from March to May this figure fell to an average of 2.7 million barrels per day.
According to data from the International Energy Agency (IEA), by mid-June, Middle Eastern producers had lost more than 1.3 billion barrels in exports.
Strategic straits, critical points for world trade
The Strait of Hormuz is one of the most important corridors for global oil supplies. At its narrowest point, it is about 33 kilometers wide, while the shipping lanes in each direction are only about 3.2 kilometers.
According to reports, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps has imposed strict controls on the passage of ships in the area, requiring permission from Iranian authorities to navigate in certain corridors.
The British Maritime Transport Agency (UKMTO) has recorded 23 attacks on ships in and near the strait since the beginning of October, according to reported material.
Meanwhile, threats by Houthi rebels in Yemen to maritime transport have also increased insecurity in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a strategic point that connects the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and through which commercial ships pass to the Suez Canal.
Saudi Arabia and the Emirates seek alternative routes
To limit the impact of the crisis in Hormuz, Saudi Arabia has redirected some of its oil exports through the East-West pipeline, which has a capacity of about 7 million barrels per day and ends at the port of Yanbu, on the Red Sea.
According to MEES and Kpler data, exports from Yanbu have increased from about 750 barrels per day before the war to 4 to 4.5 million barrels per day.
The pipeline was damaged in September by a drone attack. Saudi and Iraqi authorities have said the drones were launched from Iraq. Saudi Aramco has since restored the infrastructure, but at reduced capacity.
The United Arab Emirates is also using alternative infrastructure to avoid the Strait of Hormuz. The Habshan–Fujairah pipeline enables the export of about 1.8 million barrels of oil per day through the port of Fujairah, outside the strait.
According to the IEA, the Emirates' overall exports rose from 1.9 million barrels per day in March to 4.3 million in early June.
Iran, on the other hand, sends about 90 percent of its oil exports through Kharg Island. Some of the oil can also be transported through the Goreh–Jask oil pipeline, about 1.000 kilometers long, which ends at a port outside the Strait of Hormuz.
Yemen and the risk to shipping through the Red Sea
In the other strategic corridor, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, threats from Houthi rebels have affected the movement of oil tankers.
On July 20, the Houthis declared a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia. Over the following week, the number of oil tankers passing through the strait fell by 42 percent, according to data from Lloyd's List Intelligence.
The Yemeni government claimed on October 5 that it had, with support from Saudi Arabia, pushed back Houthi rebels from the coast near the strait to the Mocha area. However, Reuters has not independently verified this claim.
In the event of the closure of Bab el-Mandeb, tankers transporting oil from the port of Yanbu to Japan would be forced to follow a much longer route, through the Suez Canal and then around the Cape of Good Hope.
According to Kpler's estimates, this route is about 14.700 nautical miles, compared to 7.650 nautical miles on the alternative route described in the report. The journey could take anywhere from four to eight weeks.
An alternative for supplying Europe is to use the Suez Canal in combination with the Egyptian SUMED pipeline, which has a capacity of 2.5 million barrels per day.
Economic damage and rising oil prices
The consequences of the conflict are also being reflected in the costs of repairing energy infrastructure and in export revenues.
In March, Rystad Energy estimated that repairing oil and gas infrastructure in the region would cost at least $25 billion.
Meanwhile, Iraqi Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein stated on October 16 that Iraq had lost about $60 billion in oil export revenue due to the war.
However, Kpler data shows that in the last few days of September, Middle Eastern crude oil exports exceeded the pre-war average of 18 million barrels per day. A significant portion of the oil was transported via alternative routes.
On October 16, Brent crude oil was trading at $109.86 per barrel, while on April 30 the price had temporarily reached $126.41 per barrel.
The crisis shows how vulnerable the global economy remains to disruptions in strategic maritime corridors. Restrictions in Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb affect not only oil exports, but also transportation costs, energy prices and the supply of international markets.

articles.title: Dozens feared trapped as high-rise collapses in Kenya’s Nairobi
articles.summary: A multistory building collapsed in Kenya’s capital, Nairobi, on Friday, leaving many people feared trapped beneath massive piles of concrete as more than a dozen floors crumbled on...
articles.full_text:
A multistory building collapsed in Kenya’s capital, Nairobi, on Friday, leaving many people feared trapped beneath massive piles of concrete as more than a dozen floors crumbled on top of one another.
The building was under construction when it collapsed at about 1 p.m. along a busy commercial street in Nairobi's Eastleigh area, which is often crowded with thousands of traders and residents.
Nairobi police chief Issa Mohamud said the building had more than 10 upper floors under construction. Rescue operations were complicated, with police firing tear gas at people who had begun looting neighboring shops, as officers sought to clear the area and provide access to emergency response teams.
Joseph Kaula made it out just in time. A plasterer working on the fifth floor, he said he heard screams and spotted other workers rushing outside, shouting that the building was collapsing.
"I was the last person to walk out before it collapsed and the whole area was filled with dust,” Kaula said.
Kaula suspects a few of his colleagues were trapped in the basement.
One injured woman was rescued and hospitalized, and another person who was crying for help had gone silent, the police chief said.
Mohamud also warned of a possible secondary collapse, as the collapsed building was leaning on its neighbor.
There was little in the way of heavy equipment immediately available. Hours later, a group of rescuers in hard hats were using poles stripped from trees to poke at the huge pile of rubble. One excavator began to move concrete bound with steel away. By evening, at least two more back shovels arrived.
Rescuers were hoping to reach into any spaces left in the basement and the ground level, which had been rented out for an electronics shop, a butchery and a grocery while construction continued on the upper floors.
Residents said some of their loved ones who were trapped had made phone calls calling for help immediately after the collapse, but that their phones later became unreachable. A tent was set up where people could report the missing. How many might be inside the wreckage wasn't known.
Building collapses are a recurring problem in Nairobi . County officials responsible for issuing building permits have been accused of failing to conduct adequate inspections to ensure developers comply with safety guidelines and construction standards.
"Investigations will be carried out,” Mohamud said. "We’ll make sure people face the law for any negligence.”
Nairobi Gov. Johnson Sakaja said the building had been approved for construction, but did not have a certificate of occupation, so opening shops on the ground floor was against the law. Kenya's county governments need stronger enforcement powers, he said, arguing that lenient penalties for non-compliance are just a "slap on the wrist” for developers that violate regulations.

articles.title: London shoppers face facial scans as Oxford Street gets new cameras
articles.summary: London's busiest shopping district is set for heightened surveillance this December, as live facial recognition cameras are scheduled to be introduced along Oxford Street, potentia...
articles.full_text:
London's busiest shopping district is set for heightened surveillance this December, as live facial recognition cameras are scheduled to be introduced along Oxford Street, potentially scanning thousands of visitors during the Christmas shopping season
Oxford Street is one of the world’s busiest shopping areas, with about half a million visitors each day.
It would be among the first areas in the country to have permanent, live facial recognition (LFR) infrastructure scanning the faces of people passing through and comparing them with a watchlist of wanted suspects.
LFR has been widely criticized by human rights groups, with one organization describing the technology as "unregulated.”
The cameras will likely be installed in December, it is understood, and could be attached to street furniture such as lampposts.
It comes as a stretch of Oxford Street is due to be pedestrianized next week, with plans for the whole street to eventually become traffic-free.
The Metropolitan Police plans to use static, live, facial recognition cameras in London’s West End and Soho, which have some of the highest crime rates in London.
The U.K. government launched a public consultation in December 2025 to develop a legal framework for law enforcement use of biometrics, facial recognition and similar technologies.
The Home Office is expected to publish its response to the public consultation later this Parliamentary session.
Akiko Hart, director of human rights organization Liberty, told the Press Association: "The introduction of fixed, live, facial recognition cameras on Oxford Street will mean thousands of Christmas shoppers will have their faces scanned by this unregulated surveillance technology without being given a choice.
"Despite a public consultation on facial recognition closing in February, the government has yet to publish its response. Yet permanent, facial recognition cameras are set to be installed in one of the country’s busiest destinations without a legal framework to protect the public’s rights.
"This lack of transparency damages public trust and, until clear laws, proper safeguards and independent oversight are in place, this significant rollout should be paused.”
A Met spokesperson said: "Live, facial recognition is an important tool which is helping us keep London safe.
"Static cameras have already been piloted in Croydon for six months and contributed to a 10% reduction in crime and led to 173 arrests - one every 35 minutes. Considering this success, the public would rightly expect us to look at how we can use technology to keep the busiest parts of our capital safe.
"It is important to note that static systems are only turned on when officers are present on the ground, and signs will make it clear to the public that a deployment is taking place.
"Conversations remain ongoing with our partners on where we will place the cameras.”
Commissioner Mark Rowley, of the Met, has described LFR as "one of the most revolutionary technology advances in policing in recent years”, with the force arresting more than 2,000 people using facial recognition since the start of 2024.
The technology has also started to be deployed at London’s Tube stations.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has backed the expansion of LFR.
Speaking at the Police Federation annual conference on Thursday, she said: "We will expand live, facial recognition so that instead of spending hours and hours crawling through CCTV, you’ll get a match in seconds.”

articles.title: Russia confirms Melania Trump-brokered cease-fire in Ukraine
articles.summary: The Kremlin confirmed Friday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to a temporary cease-fire in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky following mediation efforts by U.S. firs...
articles.full_text:
The Kremlin confirmed Friday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to a temporary cease-fire in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky following mediation efforts by U.S. first lady Melania Trump, paving the way for humanitarian aid deliveries and the evacuation of civilians trapped in deteriorating conditions.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Russian and Ukrainian military officials were coordinating the timing of the localized truce, which the White House announced would begin Oct. 29.
"We welcome the efforts of U.S. First Lady Melania Trump, who has made a significant contribution to coordinating the humanitarian operation," Peskov told reporters.
He said the agreement had also been discussed during a recent telephone conversation between Russian President Vladimir Putin and U.S. President Donald Trump.
According to Peskov, all civilians wishing to leave Oleshky would be permitted to do so, with the evacuation operation expected to take several days.
The White House announced the agreement earlier Friday, saying Melania Trump had initiated discussions and worked through a representative directly with Russian and Ukrainian officials to establish the terms of the humanitarian pause.
The first lady described conditions in Oleshky as catastrophic, warning that the city was approaching a humanitarian disaster after years of fighting and severe shortages of essential supplies.
"The situation in Oleshky is dire. Oleshky is a front-line war city on the brink of disaster," she said in a statement.
Under the agreement, civilian representatives from Russia and Ukraine will visit residents to assess their humanitarian needs and coordinate assistance.
Those wishing to evacuate will receive transportation to their preferred destinations, whether in Ukrainian- or Russian-controlled territory.
"I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine," Melania Trump said.
She added that an independent American media organization would accompany the teams to document the operation and help ensure that families' wishes were respected. The organization was not identified.
There was no immediate public confirmation from Ukrainian authorities regarding the agreement.
President Donald Trump welcomed his wife's involvement, saying her priority was protecting children affected by the conflict.
"What she wants to do is save children, and that's her focus. And both sides are cooperating with her, so doing a very good job," Trump told reporters as he departed the White House.
Asked whether the first lady could participate in broader trilateral peace negotiations, Trump replied: "That is not the worst idea I've ever heard."
He said the initiative originated with Melania Trump and that both Moscow and Kyiv had responded positively to her outreach.
The first lady has made the protection of children in conflict zones a central focus of her public work, including efforts to reunite families separated by the Russia-Ukraine war.
Earlier this year, she chaired a United Nations Security Council meeting addressing the plight of children affected by armed conflicts and previously contacted Putin about efforts to reunite displaced children with their families.
Russian officials had also acknowledged contacts with her office before Friday's announcement.
Earlier this month, the Kremlin said Russian human rights ombudswoman Yana Lantratova would communicate with Melania Trump's team regarding the humanitarian situation in Oleshky.
Lantratova subsequently confirmed those contacts, while Russian state news agency Tass reported that she had discussed the situation with her Ukrainian counterpart, Dmytro Lubinets.
The cease-fire announcement comes as conditions in Oleshky, a city along the Dnipro River in southern Ukraine's Kherson region, continue to deteriorate amid prolonged Russian occupation.
Russian forces captured the city, previously home to approximately 24,000 people, during the opening days of Moscow's full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Years of fighting have devastated local infrastructure, leaving residents without reliable electricity, heating or running water.
Food and medical supplies have become increasingly scarce, while mined roads, destroyed vehicles and persistent drone activity have made movement into and out of the city extremely dangerous.
Oleshky suffered further destruction in June 2023 when floodwaters engulfed the area following the collapse of the Kakhovka Dam. An Associated Press investigation subsequently concluded that the explosion that destroyed the dam was likely caused by Russian forces.
Hundreds of residents were killed in the flooding, compounding the humanitarian consequences of the war.
With another winter approaching, civilians remaining in Oleshky face mounting risks from hunger, disease and exposure to freezing temperatures.
Ukrainian authorities have repeatedly called for a localized cease-fire to facilitate evacuations, while Russia, as the occupying power, is obligated under international humanitarian law to ensure that civilians have access to essential supplies.
The proposed humanitarian pause would provide a rare opportunity for aid organizations and civilian representatives to reach residents who have remained largely isolated by the fighting.
Although Moscow has acknowledged the agreement, its implementation will depend on military coordination between the two sides and the establishment of conditions allowing humanitarian personnel and civilians to move safely.
