articles.summary: Seven ⁠people were killed and 40 others were injured when gunmen opened fire during a funeral at a Greek Orthodox church in Jordan's Karak governorate on Friday. Security forces ha...
articles.full_text:
Seven people were killed and 40 others were injured when gunmen opened fire during a funeral at a Greek Orthodox church in Jordan's Karak governorate on Friday.
Security forces had been deployed to the church and were pursuing the suspects, the state-owned Al-Mamlaka television station reported. It said gunmen got out of a vehicle and opened fire during a funeral procession at the Hamoud Church in Karak. Al-Mamlaka previously reported seven had been killed in the attack.
Speaking at a press conference, Major General Abdallah al-Maaytah said most of those wounded in the shooting at the Hamoud Church in Karak governorate were still receiving treatment, and that the hunt for the attackers was ongoing. Jordan's health minister said 40 people were wounded.
Interior Minister Mazin Al Farrayeh said the attack had been carried out by "extremists", but that it was too early to tell whether they had any links to known groups inside or outside Jordan.
Khaled Burqan, a man who had been attending the funeral, told Al-Mamlaka that dozens of people had been attending the funeral and at least two men - one carrying a rifle and another carrying a pistol - opened fire on them for several minutes.
There was no immediate claim of responsibility for the attack and Jordanian authorities did not say who was responsible.
Jordan's King Abdullah said those behind the attack would be punished "with an iron fist."
"The terrorist attack against Karak will be met with the harshest retaliation. Those who delude themselves into thinking that they can divide Jordanians with their bullets have no chance in the face of our unity," he said in a statement.
Reuters footage from the church after the attack showed blood smeared on the floor near its entrance, where security forces were deployed.
Such attacks are extremely rare in Jordan, which is relatively stable, though Jordanian authorities say they have repeatedly foiled attempted attacks by terrorists in recent years.
Christians make up a minority of Jordan's population. The country is home to several biblical sites that attract Christian pilgrims from around the world.
Jordan's Minister of Endowments and Islamic Affairs Mohammad Khalayleh and several members of Jordan's parliament condemned the attack in comments to Al-Mamlaka.
In a post on X, United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres condemned the violence and said attacks against civilians and places of worship are unacceptable.
People who gathered at a Karak government hospital to support the wounded expressed shock.
"What happened today has left people unable to speak or raise our voices. But our only reproach to the state is that it must investigate these dark ideas - where they come from and how they enter the minds of our children," said one of them, Hani Al-Mbaydeen.
Christians make up a minority of Jordan's population. The country is home to several biblical sites that attract Christian pilgrims from around the world.
The U.S. ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz described it on X as a "depraved and brutal attack on a house of worship."

articles.title: Trump-Kim summit prospects fade as North Korea remains silent
articles.summary: The chances of a meeting between U.S. President Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un this year are fading, with Pyongyang yet to respond to Washington's outreach and li...
articles.full_text:
The chances of a meeting between U.S. President Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un this year are fading, with Pyongyang yet to respond to Washington's outreach and little time remaining before a regional summit in China where the two leaders could meet, according to five people familiar with the matter.
Trump has expressed interest in reviving diplomacy with North Korea, having met Kim three times during his first term. But Pyongyang has shown little enthusiasm for renewed talks aimed at curbing its nuclear program, leaving the prospect of another high-profile summit increasingly uncertain.
The United States has received no response to its efforts to arrange a meeting, according to the five people, four of whom were briefed by senior U.S. and South Korean officials. A South Korean official also said there were no signs that North Korea was preparing for a meeting.
The leaders could still meet on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, on Nov. 18-19, but the window for arranging such an encounter is narrowing.
In August, Trump said he planned to meet Kim later this year and indicated that the North Korean leader had responded to his outreach.
South Korea's intelligence agency told lawmakers late last month that there was a 50% chance the leaders would meet during the APEC summit. But Trump struck a more cautious tone Monday, playing down the likelihood of a meeting during the gathering or a regional summit in the Philippines later in November.
"I get along with him very well, and I'm not sure that anybody's asking for a meeting," Trump told reporters at the White House.
A White House official said Trump remained willing to engage Kim without preconditions, while emphasizing that no meeting had been scheduled.
"President Trump remains open to talking with Kim Jong Un, without any preconditions. No meetings to announce at this time. The leaders will meet at the appropriate time," the official said.
Last week, South Korean Ambassador to Washington Kang Kyung-wha said there had been no concrete progress toward a summit. A senior U.S. official had similarly said last month that Trump was ready to speak with Kim and that the initiative now rested with Pyongyang.
North Korean state media has indicated that any bilateral summit would come with tough conditions, potentially including sanctions relief. Kim's influential sister, Kim Yo Jong, has described the two leaders as having an "excellent" relationship, but that has not translated into renewed diplomatic engagement.
Ankit Panda, a senior fellow in the Nuclear Policy Program at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, estimated that the chance of a Trump-Kim meeting at the APEC summit was below 10%.
He said Pyongyang was likely seeking a significant public gesture from Washington before agreeing to another meeting, adding that a recent U.S. decision to scale back military exercises with South Korea had not been enough.
Washington has periodically sought China's help in facilitating talks with North Korea, which maintains close ties with Beijing. But cordial relations between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping have yet to produce a breakthrough with Pyongyang.
Despite three historic meetings in 2018 and 2019, Trump and Kim failed to reach a lasting agreement on North Korea's nuclear weapons program.
The two Koreas remain technically at war under the armistice that ended fighting in the 1950-53 Korean War. The United States maintains about 28,500 troops in South Korea as part of its joint defense posture against the North, which continues to develop nuclear weapons and ballistic missiles. South Korean officials have cited estimates from private research groups putting North Korea's nuclear arsenal at between 80 and 120 warheads.
U.S. Ambassador to South Korea Michelle Steel said Wednesday that the timing of any meeting remained uncertain but suggested it could come together quickly if both sides agreed.
"If it happens, then it's going to happen the next day or within a couple of days' notice," she said at an event organized by the American Chamber of Commerce in Korea.

articles.title: Pope Leo XIV skips Assisi peace meeting during cancer recovery
articles.summary: Pope Leo XIV will skip an interfaith peace gathering in the Italian town of Assisi next week as he continues recovering from lung cancer surgery, with doctors advising him against...
articles.full_text:
Pope Leo XIV will skip an interfaith peace gathering in the Italian town of Assisi next week as he continues recovering from lung cancer surgery, with doctors advising him against the helicopter journey from the Vatican.
The 71-year-old pope had been scheduled to attend Tuesday's event, titled “Disarmed and Disarming Peace,” which marks the 40th anniversary of a landmark interfaith prayer meeting convened by St. John Paul II in 1986.
The Vatican said Friday that a follow-up chest X-ray showed Leo was recovering well, but his medical team recommended avoiding the trip as a precaution because of the short time since his operation.
Instead, Leo will send a message to organizers, religious leaders and other participants, expressing his support for the gathering and reaffirming the importance of dialogue and peaceful coexistence amid ongoing conflicts.
The meeting brings together representatives of different faiths to pray for peace and renew the spirit of the 1986 gathering. Assisi, the birthplace of St. Francis of Assisi, has long served as a symbol of interfaith dialogue.
The cancellation is the latest adjustment to Leo's schedule following surgery last week to remove the lower lobe of his right lung, where doctors had found a malignant nodule. Tests confirmed adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer.
The Vatican said subsequent examinations found that the cancer was localized and that Leo would not need further treatment. His activities, however, will continue to be guided by medical advice as he recovers.
Leo returned to the Vatican on Saturday after the operation. Although he has appeared in good health during public appearances since his return, speaking clearly and with a strong voice, doctors are taking precautions while his lungs heal.
The decision to avoid the Assisi trip also comes as the pope prepares for a planned visit to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from Nov. 6 to 17. The trip is expected to involve about a dozen flights and two helicopter rides to high-altitude destinations.
His surgeon previously said there were no clinical reasons to rule out the Latin American journey. Thoracic surgeons often advise patients to avoid flying for about three weeks after lung surgery, a recovery period that would leave Leo little margin before his scheduled departure.
The Vatican said the pope remains close to those attending the Assisi gathering and believes its message is particularly relevant at a time of international conflict.

articles.title: Earthquake kills 16, injures 76 in Tibet as rescue efforts continue
articles.summary: A magnitude 7 earthquake in Tibet has killed at least 16 people and injured 76, with hundreds of homes destroyed as rescuers search remote, high-altitude communities for survivors...
articles.full_text:
A magnitude 7 earthquake in Tibet has killed at least 16 people and injured 76, with hundreds of homes destroyed as rescuers search remote, high-altitude communities for survivors amid freezing temperatures, dangerous aftershocks and rockslides.
Rescue teams have searched villages and damaged homes in China's Tibet region after a magnitude 7 earthquake killed at least 16 people, injured 76 and forced more than 12,000 residents to evacuate, state media and local officials said Friday.
The earthquake struck Nagqu, a sparsely populated city in northern Tibet about 4,800 meters (15,750 feet) above sea level, late Thursday. At least 339 homes collapsed, while other buildings developed cracks or began leaning, raising fears they could fall during aftershocks.
Authorities warned that the remote terrain, low temperatures and potential rockslides were complicating rescue operations. Intermittent snowfall is forecast over the next three days, adding to concerns for residents displaced by the disaster.
Nagqu's acting mayor, identified by his surname, Dunzhu, said rescuers had completed three rounds of searches by Friday afternoon, checking individual households and villages for survivors.
More than 5,000 people from three local counties were deployed to support the response. Authorities also sent more than 300 police officers, including traffic and community police, to assess damage, assist evacuations and help residents reach safer locations.
Emergency supplies arriving in the region included 2,000 prefabricated housing units, about 3,400 tents, 2,000 folding beds, flashlights and winter clothing.
More than 12,000 people had been safely relocated, according to the official Xinhua News Agency. Videos released by local media showed residents fleeing their homes and taking shelter outdoors or in parked cars as the earthquake shook buildings.
The U.S. Geological Survey said the earthquake occurred at 10:33 p.m. Thursday local time, with its epicenter 191 kilometers (119 miles) east-northeast of Nagqu and a depth of 18 kilometers (11 miles).
China's Earthquake Networks Center reported 413 aftershocks. The U.S. agency separately recorded at least seven aftershocks measuring between magnitude 4.3 and 5.2, each at a depth of about 10 kilometers (6 miles).
The tremors and resulting rockfalls disrupted transportation and communications. Local railway authorities halted trains passing through the affected region, while officials closed part of National Highway 317 to clear debris. Only emergency, rescue and official support vehicles were permitted through the restricted section.
Communication and power supplies were gradually being restored, local officials said.
Chinese President Xi Jinping called Friday for all-out rescue operations and medical assistance, underscoring the seriousness of the disaster.
The earthquake was China's strongest since a magnitude 7.1 tremor struck neighboring Qinghai province in January 2024, according to the report. A magnitude 7.1 earthquake hit Yushu in Qinghai in 2010, killing at least 2,698 people and leaving nearly 300 others missing.

articles.title: Ukrainian soldier clings to hope of seeing his children after surgery
articles.summary: Mykola Kasiuk refused to give up on his remaining eye, even after doctors told him he had lost his sight and recommended removing it. Two years after a land mine left him nearly bl...
articles.full_text:
Mykola Kasiuk refused to give up on his remaining eye, even after doctors told him he had lost his sight and recommended removing it. Two years after a land mine left him nearly blind, the Ukrainian soldier was placing his hopes in a team of U.S. surgeons working to repair the damage.
Lying in a hospital bed in Kyiv before surgery, Kasiuk crossed himself and prayed.
“I want to be able to see my children again,” he said.
Russia’s war in Ukraine has left soldiers and civilians with devastating eye and facial injuries, while specialists capable of treating complex cases remain scarce.
Before Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, eye care at many Ukrainian hospitals was largely limited to routine procedures such as cataract surgery.
A visiting team of American surgeons is helping fill that gap by treating severely injured patients and training Ukrainian doctors in oculoplastic surgery, which repairs the structures around the eyes. The procedures range from reconstructing damaged eye sockets and eyelids to fitting artificial eyes.
For Kasiuk, the operation offered a chance to preserve an eye that local doctors had considered beyond saving.
“No, I won’t let them,” he told his wife, Tetyana, when she relayed the recommendation to remove it. “This is my last hope.”
Kasiuk had trained as a military cook, not an infantryman. But after joining the military, he was given a rifle and sent into some of the fiercest fighting in eastern Ukraine.
His final memories of the world around him are scenes of devastation in the Donetsk region: fellow soldiers killed in combat, homes reduced to rubble and dogs wandering through the ruins. He remembers hearing Russian soldiers nearby and the pervasive smell of death.
On April 16, 2024, Kasiuk was walking with fellow soldiers when he stepped on something and fell. His commanders later told Tetyana that he had triggered a land mine.
The evacuation vehicle carrying him came under fire. Almost everyone inside was killed.
When Tetyana arrived at the hospital, she struggled to recognize the swollen, bandaged man covered in shrapnel wounds. His teeth had been shattered, and his face was barely recognizable.
“This is not my husband,” she told a hospital attendant.
Then she noticed the tattoos on his hands. They were his.
Doctors removed one eye after shrapnel pierced it and raised concerns about infection. They operated on the other but suspected the optic nerve had been damaged. Kasiuk was transferred between hospitals and underwent repeated operations, with little improvement in his vision.
He gradually learned to navigate life without sight. He uses an old mobile phone to make calls and listen to the news, and recently learned to style his own hair. When Tetyana switches on a lamp, he tells her that the faint light he can still perceive becomes brighter.
That small trace of vision has kept hope alive.
The American surgeons came to Kyiv through Vision for Ukraine, a medical mission organized by the Christian Medical Association of Ukraine. They would not know the full extent of the damage until they operated on Kasiuk’s eye socket.
Stuart Seiff, an oculoplastic surgeon from San Francisco, approached the case cautiously. The immediate priority was to reconstruct the socket and eyelids, improve the eye’s protection and restore some of Kasiuk’s appearance and sense of normality.
“The socket on the right is very contracted,” Seiff said.
Surgeons can rebuild the damaged lining using tissue taken from inside the mouth or behind the ear, or a specially prepared amniotic membrane that helps healing and reduces scarring. If vision cannot be restored, an artificial eye can provide a more natural appearance.
That was the outcome for Artem Deresh, another wounded Ukrainian soldier. His prosthetic eye, meticulously hand-painted in a Kyiv laboratory, looks almost real.
“I don’t want to stand out from the crowd. I also don’t want to make people uncomfortable,” Deresh said.
For Kasiuk, the stakes extended beyond his appearance. He wanted to regain even a small measure of independence and, if possible, see his family again.
On the day of surgery, a nurse helped him into scrubs and wheeled him toward the operating room. He prayed aloud along the way, repeatedly asking questions about the procedure and whether it would work.
The nurse tried to reassure him, telling him not to worry and that he would be beautiful.
The operation unfolded under the constant threat of Russian attacks. An air-raid alert interrupted the hospital’s routine, potentially delaying procedures for hours. When the alert ended, applause broke out across the ward as staff rushed to resume their work.
During the hourslong operation, a major strike hit Kyiv’s National Sciences Building, sending plumes of smoke into the air. Hours later, another strike hit a medical facility in the city.
Back home in Chernivtsi, in western Ukraine, Tetyana waited anxiously, knowing that the surgeons’ findings could shape the family’s future.
The man she had known before the war was gone, she said. Kasiuk had worked in factories to support the family, and together they had raised three daughters.
“He lives in his own little world now,” Tetyana said.
Kasiuk lives with almost constant pain, and his days and nights have lost their rhythm. Sometimes he sleeps through the day and remains awake all night.
His daughters are growing up, each moving toward a future he cannot see. His eldest is studying psychology, while his middle daughter is pursuing art and has won awards for her paintings. The youngest, now in sixth grade, remembers a father who could see, play with his children and take them on trips.
His condition has traumatized the children, Tetyana said.
She tries to shield her husband from worries she fears he cannot bear while navigating disability paperwork, pursuing further treatment and holding the family together. The burden has left her exhausted.
“Sometimes I wish someone would understand that I get tired, too,” she said.
The surgeons found more potential for recovery than they had expected.
They restored movement in Kasiuk’s eye and used skin grafted from behind his ear to help the eyelid protect it. The procedure also opened the possibility of a corneal transplant.
“He has a fantastic result at this point, absolutely fantastic,” Seiff said.
Whether Kasiuk will regain his sight remains uncertain. Doctors suspect scarring on the cornea, the transparent front surface of the eye, is clouding his vision. They still do not know how much damage lies deeper inside the eye or whether it can transmit visual signals to the brain.
His recovery will depend partly on how the eye heals. Scar tissue could form again and cloud the cornea, potentially undermining the gains made during surgery.
“That’s the big enemy. We try to control it, but there’s only so much you can do,” Seiff said.
Doctors plan to monitor Kasiuk for up to six months before deciding whether he needs another intervention. Options could include using stem cells to support a corneal transplant or implanting an artificial cornea.
For now, Kasiuk is holding on to the possibility that some of the world he remembers might return.
“I remember what the world looked like: the sun, the blue sky, the clouds,” he said. “I hope I’ll be able to see this beautiful world again, even if only a little.”

articles.title: Nurseries offer lifeline to DR Congo’s youngest Ebola victims
articles.summary: A caregiver wearing a protective gown and gloves bottle-fed a baby, one of hundreds of children orphaned by the Democratic Republic of Congo’s Ebola outbreak. Five months into the...
articles.full_text:
A caregiver wearing a protective gown and gloves bottle-fed a baby, one of hundreds of children orphaned by the Democratic Republic of Congo’s Ebola outbreak.
Five months into the epidemic, the virus continues to spread, and the nursery in the country’s remote east is among 12 facilities caring for children whose parents have died from the highly contagious disease.
“Many children have lost both their father and mother because of Ebola,” Marie Bakikula, a caregiver at a UNICEF-supported nursery in Mongbwalu, told Agence France-Presse (AFP).
The mining town in Ituri province, near the Ugandan border, is considered the epicenter of the outbreak.
Children account for about one-third of deaths and more than one-quarter of infections in the current crisis, which has recorded more than 2,000 cases, according to UNICEF.
A short distance from the nursery, workers in white protective suits loaded a child-sized coffin into the back of a pickup truck.
Other children survive but lose their families. Those arriving at the emergency nurseries have witnessed their parents die and seen burial teams in protective suits remove their bodies.
Others were separated from their families after their infected parents were transferred to Ebola treatment centers.
“They all believe that by coming here they will never see their parents again,” said Monique Ndjangosi, a psychologist at the Mongbwalu nursery.
Nearby, a young girl and three boys played among stuffed toys that had recently been disinfected with chlorine. Their mothers had tested positive for the virus.
The children will remain under observation for 21 days, the disease’s incubation period, in case they develop symptoms.
“One of them showed symptoms seven days after arriving and was admitted to the Ebola treatment center,” said Bakikula, who volunteered to work at the facility after surviving Ebola herself.
The only contact many children maintain with their infected parents is through photographs and videos taken by health care workers.
“We cannot take them inside the treatment center to visit their parents. It’s too risky,” Ndjangosi said.
In some cases, child protection teams succeed in locating relatives, including distant family members, who can care for orphaned children. In others, finding relatives proves impossible.
“We still have children we have not been able to identify because they are too young and their parents arrived in a coma,” said Celine Lusinde, head of provincial child protection services.
Her office has registered 8,200 newly orphaned children since the outbreak began.
Marie-Therese Tsesi, a 63-year-old nurse, has taken in five children orphaned by Ebola at her modest mud-brick home near Mongbwalu hospital.
“Their father was the only parent they had left. He died of Ebola,” she said.
“They were sleeping outside and showing signs of malnutrition.”
The current Ebola epidemic, the Democratic Republic of Congo’s 17th, quickly became the deadliest on record in the central African country and remains uncontrolled despite months of efforts. Cases have also been detected in Uganda, Kenya and Nigeria.
The disease spreads through contact with bodily fluids and causes severe hemorrhagic fever. It has infected 9,704 people and killed 4,687 in the DRC, according to the latest health authority figures, giving it a fatality rate of nearly 50%.
A clinical trial is underway, but there is currently no approved vaccine or specific treatment for the Bundibugyo strain responsible for the outbreak.
Health authorities continue to face resource shortages, while insecurity caused by armed groups in Ituri province, the area hardest hit by the epidemic, restricts access to some communities.
Many deaths occurring outside health facilities are believed to go unreported.

articles.title: War-ravaged Sudan on brink as El Nino fans new flames of hunger
articles.summary: Farmers across Sudan are facing a devastating harvest as drought and soaring temperatures compound the effects of a civil war that has already pushed millions toward hunger, raisin...
articles.full_text:
Farmers across Sudan are facing a devastating harvest as drought and soaring temperatures compound the effects of a civil war that has already pushed millions toward hunger, raising fears of a worsening famine.
El Nino, the climate pattern threatening parts of Africa with extreme weather, has brought higher temperatures and drought to Sudan, where pockets of famine have emerged during more than three years of fighting.
Rain-fed agriculture, which supplies much of the country’s food, is suffering as crops wither, livestock weaken and farmers struggle to salvage their fields.
Rainfall during July through September, Sudan’s peak rainy season, was the lowest in more than three decades nationwide, according to U.S. Geological Survey data.
North Darfur recorded its lowest rainfall since 1984, the year a devastating famine struck Sudan and Ethiopia. North Kordofan experienced its lowest rainfall since 1990, while southeastern Gedaref state recorded its lowest since 1991.
“The risk of famine is growing in many conflict-affected areas of Sudan, with the impact of El Nino-induced drought compounding already dire conditions,” the U.N.-backed Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) said in an Oct. 12 alert.
In June, the IPC estimated that 5.1 million people faced severe hunger. The figure is being updated, but the drought threatens to reverse expected improvements as the harvest season begins.
The World Food Program forecasts that drought will leave an additional 350,000 people facing severe hunger by the end of 2026, rising to 1.2 million more by August 2027, Samuel Clendon, the agency’s head of program for Sudan, told Reuters in October. Darfur and Kordofan are expected to be hardest hit.
Crops wither as livestock lose value
In North Kordofan, Mariam Omar pulls weeds from her smallholding near Um Ruwaba, where crops that should be nearing harvest have shriveled in the dry, sandy soil.
“This year is terrible,” she said.
Mohamed Abdelrahman, a farmer who operates about 420 hectares and finances smallholders through his sesame trading business, estimated that about 40% of farmland around Um Ruwaba would produce no harvest. Many farmers displaced by the war are returning to drought-stricken land, he said.
Livestock markets are also suffering. At El Obeid, North Kordofan’s capital, cows stand with their ribs protruding beneath dusty hides.
“Usually at this time the cattle are fat and everyone is making a profit. But now, with this autumn’s scarcity, the cattle became skinny,” trader Sirajaldeen Abdellateef said.
A rapidly depreciating currency and rising inflation are adding to farmers’ losses, making food and other essentials increasingly expensive.
The WFP has prioritized 5 million people most in need but says it cannot reach everyone requiring assistance. For those it serves, the agency has cut food rations to stretch limited supplies.
As of Oct. 17, the WFP had $276 million available for its Sudan operation, less than half of last year’s budget. It needs another $134 million to address hunger caused by drought.
The simultaneous decline in food aid and agricultural production is a “recipe for disaster,” the WFP’s acting executive director, Carl Skau, told Reuters after visiting Darfur.
In Tawila, a sprawling Darfur displacement camp sheltering about 700,000 people, food rations have been halved even as thousands more arrive, Skau said. Aid workers reported that 9,000 people reached the camp between early September and mid-October.
Suad Ahmed, a teacher who has been displaced several times during the war, fled her village east of al-Fashir, North Darfur’s capital, to seek food in Tawila.
“As I was coming here on the road, so many people said: ‘If you find food and drink there, please tell us,’” she said.
Adam Rojal, spokesman for the General Coordination of Displaced Persons and Refugee Camps in Sudan, said hunger was increasingly driving people from their homes.
“It’s no longer just about bullets,” he said.
Even Gedaref, a southeastern state that has largely escaped the fighting and become an important source of food during the war, has been hit by drought.
Emad Kabsoor, who operates farms covering 14,700 hectares, said scorching temperatures and a lack of rain had devastated his fields.
“Even if we get rain going forward, I’ll only have about 25% of last year’s crop,” he said. “We’ve never had a season like this.”
Temperatures in Gedaref on Oct. 20 were between 7 and 9 degrees Celsius above the historical average, according to the Reuters Climate Monitor.
Sudan’s government has downplayed the threat. Agriculture Minister Esmat Qureshi said Oct. 8 that this year’s harvest would be smaller but “not significantly less than last year’s.”
The drought is worsening conditions in a country where fighting between the military and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) has devastated communities, disrupted agriculture and displaced millions.
Humanitarian agencies have repeatedly accused both sides of blocking or hindering aid deliveries. Both deny the allegations.
Abdelrahman Ismail, head of the RSF’s humanitarian aid authority, told Reuters the group had sought to coordinate an early response and could do more with sufficient resources.
The IPC declared pockets of famine in Sudan in 2024 and 2025, including in al-Fashir, where government forces and their allies, along with as many as 250,000 civilians, endured an RSF siege for about 18 months before the city fell.
Famine expert Alex de Waal said Sudan’s current crisis was in many respects worse than the famine that devastated the region in 1984, killing hundreds of thousands. While the international community mobilized substantial assistance then, humanitarian budgets are now being cut.
“The situation today is in most respects much, much worse because of the conflict,” de Waal said.
Sirajaldin al-Tahir, a farmer in Um Ruwaba, remembers the 1984 famine, when failed harvests and dying livestock forced people to flee. He said U.S. food aid helped his village survive.
“But God took pity on us, and the US government brought in aid and distributed it to our village,” he said.
More than four decades later, failed rains and collapsing harvests are again threatening Sudan’s food supply, while war and shrinking aid budgets leave millions increasingly vulnerable.
“This year, 2026, we don’t know how it will end,” al-Tahir said.

articles.title: Macron faces tall order as France braces for renewed protests
articles.summary: France was bracing Friday for another weekend of protests after demonstrations a week earlier descended into some of the country’s worst urban violence in years, prompting Presiden...
articles.full_text:
France was bracing Friday for another weekend of protests after demonstrations a week earlier descended into some of the country’s worst urban violence in years, prompting President Emmanuel Macron to step up efforts to restore order and regain control of the crisis.
Macron, who announced Thursday that only trade union-organized demonstrations would be permitted this weekend, was scheduled to convene his defense council of senior ministers and officials before meeting with security forces.
He was also due to meet representatives of high school students for the first time. Protests over school conditions, initially driven by students, have since spread nationwide, evolving into a broader expression of public anger over the government and the rising cost of living.
The unrest has erupted at a critical moment for France, just six months before elections to choose Macron’s successor. A new poll showed far-right candidate Marine Le Pen leading the race, with the latest developments further strengthening her position.
Adding to tensions, Le Pen was due to host her National Rally (RN) party congress in Orleans over the weekend, with thousands of supporters expected. Local authorities feared clashes as opponents headed to the city.
Macron was due to announce “additional decisions” after the defense council meeting, on top of the limited curfews already announced, his office said.
At the meeting with students, “we will present our demands to him, which remain the same: the state of school infrastructure and an overhaul of the Parcoursup (university admissions) system,” Nathanael Combary, president of Renouveau Lyceen (High School Renewal), told Agence France-Presse (AFP).
Pierre Sourzat, who heads Les Lyceens (The High School Students), was skeptical.
“He’ll listen to us, pretend he’s understood us, and then nothing will come of it,” Sourzat said.
Macron’s government has sought to distinguish between the legitimate demands of protesters and the looting, arson and ransacking that erupted on the sidelines of demonstrations last Saturday.
In a judicial response of unprecedented firmness, courts have already sentenced 217 people, half of them first-time offenders, to prison over Saturday’s violence, Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin said.
On Thursday, Macron called for “the utmost severity” against “acts of delinquency,” accusing “ultra-left” groups of seeking to “bring down the republic” last weekend.
Demonstrations in Marseille in the south and Lyon in the southeast were banned for the weekend, while in Paris, protesters would be allowed to march only along a limited route between Bastille and Nation squares.
Marseille authorities, however, reversed a decision to suspend all public transportation in the city Saturday. In the capital, leading museums, including the Louvre, were to close Saturday, while the Art Basel art fair was being cut short.
About 20% more security personnel were to be deployed this weekend following heavy criticism of police preparedness and intelligence gathering ahead of last week’s violence.
“In a country governed by the rule of law, the police have a responsibility both to ensure that protests can take place peacefully and safely and to protect the public from violent disorder,” said Eva Cosse, senior Europe researcher at Human Rights Watch. She also expressed alarm over reports of children being seriously injured by crowd-control weapons.
The violence has tarnished France’s image ahead of elections that could mark a turning point in its modern history, while the government’s growing debt burden has also unsettled investors.
A Harris Interactive poll for M6/RTL conducted after the violence showed Le Pen surging to 33% to 35% in the first round of the presidential election.
The poll projected that far-left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon would face Le Pen in a runoff, where she would win decisively with about 70% of the vote.
